title: `page_sidebar` and `page_navbar` should drop `sidebar` parameter and accept `Sidebar` objects in `*args`
description:
Currently, `page_sidebar()` and `page_navbar()` take an explicit `sidebar` argument.

However, for `page_auto()`, which is used in Express mode, there's no `sidebar` argument (because children can't be passed as named arguments in Express). Instead, we inspect the `*args`, pull out any `Sidebar` objects, and then explicitly pass them to the `sidebar` argument.

https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/blob/a020af6e9428b7f6780697840434ea6574f3dcec/shiny/ui/_page.py#L529-L530

Also, because of how Python handles named and unnamed ages:

- For `page_sidebar()`, the signature is `page_sidebar(sidebar, *args)`. This means that the sidebar **must** be the first argument and **must not** be named.
- For `page_navbar()`, the signature is `page_navbar(*args, sidebar)`. This means that the sidebar **must not** be the first argument, and **must** be named.

I think we should remove the `sidebar` parameter from these functions and simply inspect the `*args` for `Sidebar` objects -- essentially, take the logic from `page_auto()` and move it into `page_sidebar()` and `page_navbar()`.

title: For `page_sidebar` and `page_navbar`, consider changing default for `fillable` to `False`
description: For Express mode we had set the default page type to `page_fillable()`, but changed it back to `page_fixed()` for reasons explained in #886. In Express mode, when a sidebar is added, it uses `page_sidebar()`, which defaults to `fillable=True` and then runs into the same problem. That means that from the user's perspective, simply adding a sidebar makes a big change in how the main content of the page is laid out, and can lead to surprising errors. For example: Then the user needs to know to use `ui.page_opts(fillable=False)` to fix it. Especially in cases where there is a lot of content on the page, I think it would be very surprising for a user that simply adding a sidebar would result in this change; and then in order to understand the fix, they would need to understand the fillable concept, and that the sidebar changes the default behavior of it.

title: Think about respecting .env files
description:
There's a (not-Python-specific) convention of specifying environment variable values in .env files (that are usually git ignored) in the root of a project. Shiny app developers may want to use them to specify environment variables that will be provided by the host environment when deployed to the server. For example: https://docs.posit.co/connect/user/content-settings/#content-vars

Uvicorn has an `--env-file` argument, if this is used then the [python-dotenv](https://pypi.org/project/python-dotenv/) package needs to be installed. Perhaps we should have `shiny run` detect the presence of an .env file and pass it to Uvicorn, by default?

In the current development version of Shiny (after the 0.6.1 release), we have updated the examples so that they no longer use the `@output` decorator (#790). ```py # Old version of code examples @output @render.plot def plt(): ... # New version of code examples @render.plot def plt(): ... ``` If you have copied and pasted code that _does not_ have `@output`, and are using Shiny 0.5.1 or older, then you might have the problem shown in the screenshot above. title: Express: provide way to use render functions later?
description:
Hey--I've been loving express mode! One challenge is that often I don't want to define server logic inside the thick of a shiny express app. This is the case as the pieces in an app increase.

To workaround it, I noticed I can define a simple function (called `punt()` below) that just wraps the rendered function. Then, by using `punt()` as a decorator, I can use the rendered function later in the app.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import random

from shiny import reactive, render, ui
from shiny.express import input


# server ----
def punt(f):
    return lambda: f


@reactive.Calc
def x():
    return [random.uniform(0, 1) for _ in range(input.n_samples())]


@punt
@render.plot
def plot():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    # Histogram of the random numbers with the selected color
    ax.hist(x(), color=input.selected_color())
    return fig


# dashboard ----

ui.panel_title("PyShiny App")
ui.input_slider("n_samples", "N Samples", 10, 100, 50)
ui.input_select("selected_color", "Color", ["red", "green", "blue"])


"""IT'S PLOT TIME Y'ALL"""

plot()

```

I wonder if it would be useful to have something like this in express mode (or maybe it already exists)? What I like about it is that--unlike traditional shiny apps--it's quick to tab complete the output (e.g. `plot()` produces the output in the UI, rather than having to wire up strings).

I suspect if express apps use context managers, it will feel cumbersome to define render functions in a highly indented place.

In any event, the way express works seems great--and the punt function works as is, so no need to roll it in if not useful. I thought it might be helpful to check though on whether this seems like a reasonable approach, or an abuse of express apps 😬 .

**edit:**

alternatively, it looks like people can leave the `render.plot` decorator off, and use it later (which seems pretty nice):

```python
def plot():
    ...
    return fig

# App stuff

...

render.plot(plot)
```

title: input_handler.input_handlers documentation appears misrendered
description: The documentation provided in the source code for [`input_handler.input_handlers`](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/blob/ceb6311fa1664ee359425e7f04fca0edcaba139c/shiny/input_handler.py#L42) appears to be misrendered on [the website](https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/input_handler.input_handlers.html): * The initial paragraphs, which provide a description, are missing. * The methods table renders as a paragraph, but seems intended to be a table. Here is the source code: ```` input_handlers.__doc__ = """ Manage Shiny input handlers. Add and/or remove input handlers of a given ``type``. Shiny uses these handlers to pre-process input values from the client (after being deserialized) before passing them to the ``input`` argument of an :func:`~shiny.App`'s ``server`` function. The ``type`` is based on the ``getType()`` JavaScript method on the relevant Shiny input binding. See `this article `_ for more information on how to create custom input bindings. (The article is about Shiny for R, but the JavaScript and general principles are the same.) Methods -------- add(type: str, force: bool = False) -> Callable[[InputHandlerType], None] Register an input handler. This method returns a decorator that registers the decorated function as the handler for the given ``type``. This handler should accept three arguments: - the input ``value`` - the input ``name`` - the :class:`~shiny.Session` object remove(type: str) Unregister an input handler. Note ---- ``add()`` ing an input handler will make it persist for the duration of the Python process (unless Shiny is explicitly reloaded). For that reason, verbose naming is encouraged to minimize the risk of colliding with other Shiny input binding(s) which happen to use the same ``type`` (if this the binding is bundled with a package, we recommend the format of "packageName.widgetName"). title: `as_fillable_container()` and `as_fill_item()` should append fillability classes
description:
Currently, `ui.fill.as_fillable_container()` and `ui.fill.as_fill_item()` prepend the fill/fillable classes to the modified element's class list. ```python from shiny import ui from htmltools import div ui.fill.as_fill_item(div(class_="my-item")) #>
ui.fill.as_fillable_container(div(class_="my-container")) #>
``` As utility classes, these classes should be appended rather the prepended. In CSS the final styles are not impacted by the order of the classes in the class attribute. So this recommendation is a stylistic decision but important for debugging -- most often the first classes carry the most signal, e.g. `bslib-grid` or `bslib-sidebar-layout`, and it's much easier to debug markup in the browser when they appear first in the classlist. ```python from shiny import ui from htmltools import div ui.fill.as_fill_item(div(class_="my-item")) #>
ui.fill.as_fillable_container(div(class_="my-container")) #>
```

title: [bug]`ui.input_file` Accept Parameter Not Working with Multiple Extensions in PyShiny
description:
Hi!

Hi Folks!
In PyShiny, the `accept` parameter in `ui.input_file` does not work as expected when multiple file extensions are specified (e.g., `.tar.gz`). When set to `.tar.gz`, the input does not accept any files, suggesting an issue with handling multiple extensions. In contrast, single extensions (like `.gz`) work correctly. Additionally, setting `accept` to `tar.gz` (without the leading dot) results in the app accepting all file types, and the validation fails silently without any warnings or errors.

**Steps to Reproduce:**
1. Use the following minimal code to create a simple PyShiny app with a file input:
   ```python
   from shiny import App, ui

   app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
       ui.input_file('file', "Upload File", accept=".tar.gz")
   )

   def server(input, output, session):
       pass

   app = App(app_ui, server)
   ```
2. Attempt to upload a `.tar.gz` file.
3. Observe that the file is not accepted.
4. Change `accept` parameter to `tar.gz` and attempt to upload any file type.
5. Notice that all files are accepted, and no error is thrown.

`shiny==0.6.0`

**Expected Behavior:**
The `ui.input_file` should only accept files with the specified extensions (`.tar.gz`) and reject others. It should fail on startup with wrong `accept` parameter (like `tar.gz`).

**Actual Behavior:**
The `ui.input_file` does not accept any files when multiple extensions are specified and fails silently without validation when the extension is provided without a leading dot.

Best!

title: Consider renaming `shiny.express.layout`
description:
The name `layout` seems to be over-optimizing for `with layout.sidebar()`. It gets awkward with things like `layout.layout_*()`, `layout.page_*()`, etc.

I think I like `ux` as an alternative. Here are some pros/cons I can think of:

#### Pros

* Short and similar to `ui`, which helps with the mental model of "use `ux` as an alternative of `ui` when you want to use `@render.*` decorators as children"
* Serves as a more general home for UI things that might not be `layout` related.

### Cons

* It's maybe too similar to `ui` (hurts readability), but the fact that `ux` things will always start `with ux` will provide a clear enough distinction.

title: Consider making `page_fillable()` the default for `shiny.express`

title: Async reactive functions run sequentially instead of concurrently
description:
In previous versions of Shiny, it did the following for async reactive functions:

- Within a session, async reactive functions _within_ ran sequentially. This was done to prevent a reactive flush from being run while another flush is happening.
- Across sessions, async functions ran concurrently. We decided this was safe, as long as there were no top-level async reactives which caused a flush in the middle of another flush.

It turns out that, as of now, both of these situations run async reactives sequentially. This is safe, but it also eliminates the performance benefits from async code.

This is a test app that demonstrates the issue. If you run the app and visit it with two browsers, and click on the button in each, you can see that the async `render.text`s run sequentially instead of concurrently.

```py
import asyncio
from shiny import App, Inputs, Outputs, Session, reactive, render, ui

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.output_text("id"),
    ui.input_action_button("button", "Compute"),
    ui.output_text("compute1"),
)

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    # Get first 5 characters from Session
    id_num = session.id[:5]

    @render.text
    def id():
        return f"This session has ID: {id_num}"

    @render.text
    @reactive.event(input.button)
    async def compute1():
        for _ in range(8):
            print(f"... computing for ID {id_num}")
            await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
        return f"Finished run {input.button()} for ID {id_num}"

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/assets/86978/2eb987b7-3c0f-4df0-9f2c-a456332d2a9a


However, if we go into `shiny/session/_session.py` and comment out the following `async with lock`, then the two can run concurrently:
https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/blob/351598bc41b1eec3d2068b7f75ec874b76eca498/shiny/session/_session.py#L272


https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/assets/86978/c389da5f-7372-4d6d-b201-78b8187552cc

That `async with lock` was added in [4a0e5bff](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/commit/4a0e5bff7ff4a9eacffe5fcb8448d1265782b8fa#diff-593b4caeaea701b19634390e87e303e7003164d20d3afa0f773e085f3e0d39d1R195).

title: Express: Support trailing semicolon as a signal to not display that expression
description:
In Jupyter, you can give an expression a trailing semicolon to suppress display.
```python
"hello";
```
will show nothing.

Below is some code, inspired by [IPython.core.displayhook](https://github.com/ipython/ipython/blob/86d44b7f4674d5bf830afea5e6235c28a4b56bfd/IPython/core/displayhook.py#L97), that will determine if an AST node has a trailing semicolon. (This information is not included in the AST so we have to go back and tokenize the source code.)

This should be very easy to integration into `@display_body`/`@render.display` because those functions already descend down to the level of each auto-displayed expression and wrap them with `sys.displayhook()`. This code can be used to decide on a node-by-node basis whether to skip that transformation.

However, it's not as easy with `shiny.express._run`, which executes e.g. `with sidebar():` and its contents as a single top-level node. In order to support the semicolon check, we'd have to either do more AST transformation up front, or change the implementation of `shiny.express._run` to work more like `@display_body`.

```python
def expr_ends_in_semicolon(node: ast.AST, filename: str) -> bool:
    if node.end_lineno is None:
        return False

    end_line: int = node.end_lineno

    last_line = linecache.getline(filename, end_line)
    if last_line == "":
        # The line could not be loaded (file not found?)
        return False

    # Do a cheap check first
    if ";" not in last_line:
        return False

    def lines():
        lineno = node.lineno
        while lineno <= end_line:
            line = linecache.getline(filename, lineno)
            # if lineno == node.end_lineno:
            #     line = line[: node.end_col_offset]
            if lineno == node.lineno:
                line = line[node.col_offset :]
            yield line
            lineno += 1
        yield ""

    gen_lines = lines()

    tokens = list(tokenize.generate_tokens(lambda: next(gen_lines, "")))

    for token in reversed(tokens):
        if token[0] in (
            tokenize.ENDMARKER,
            tokenize.NL,
            tokenize.NEWLINE,
            tokenize.COMMENT,
        ):
            continue
        if (token[0] == tokenize.OP) and (token[1] == ";"):
            return True
        else:
            return False

    return False
```

The dropdown menu appears _within_ the card element, rather than an overlay that extends beyond the limits of the card (the behavior exhibited by `ui.input_select()`). This makes the card scrollable, and it's difficult to select from the dropdown menu. I'm not a CSS expert, but I think this might be related to the [z-index](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/z-index) property? Please see the example below, which illustrates the issue: ```python from shiny import Inputs, Outputs, Session, App, ui CHOICES = [f"Option {i}" for i in range(10)] app_ui = ui.page_fluid( ui.card( ui.card_header("Helloooo"), ui.input_select("success", "Dropdown overlays card:", choices=CHOICES), ui.input_selectize("failure", "Dropdown within card:", choices=CHOICES) ) ) def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session): pass app = App(app_ui, server) ```

title: Add `minview` and `maxview` arguments to date inputs
description:
First, a big thanks for bringing Shiny to Python! 🎉 

This is a feature request to add new arguments to the `input_date()` and `input_date_range()` UI components. The `minview` and `maxview` arguments would set the minimum and maximum view mode of the datepicker object. From the end-user perspective, they constrain the selectable dates:
* `minview` sets the temporal resolution the user can select. Very helpful if you want the end-user to input a month (`minview = "months"`) or year (`minview = "years"`).
* `maxview` prevents zooming-out too far, depending on context. This can make UI navigation less error-prone.

*Note:* I chose the argument names based on the existing `startview` argument.

title: Create outputs programmatically or at runtime

description:
A [question came up on the community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/return-points-selected-using-plotly-in-shiny-for-python/174555) site and in Discord about how to return selected points from a Plotly widget. Joe came up with [this solution](https://shinylive.io/py/editor/#-li6AcQcdwedLhBKXTzZSmBgISo0HBKQBaCVI2U6j7AE00zV+HTanFLEQCVBFL3DeZkOEwEQugPDYioFNQJjpvJ2GBwgDMtOu0HQgUq2sqWCgekC3DYlW0lOMdA7-CEGBEnTIgUIKjghGmIWIecMYFUxA0jYBk7yk9JKhnfwBFF+wLgC-kPL4cDhass+9l7c7xHafbGjTIbanhA+Iy8k9PEFDJg--ABfUr30ogYhhGa9ejvOCPMsZ98GUOjHi8FbBIkYgRAMbUvBkQIfw4YpIMpHaEOOpCktIvVTuIgABAoimZOAMAYbhuGHMhKK-OhAkdaCzuIl7EKkDBPpNDAFGEEIOG1QCkrGudb2+zs-sKR6ymB0Hwch1KJEsS67q2cG4G0QILEugRYd61A6fIF1gDZ8gOeVU6MRpm7sAZh6SlISkyH8KKaTh4iRFUqLnARf6yaBgA1PcvWAIV3xImnSEl8Gnrl+M8gFgw8nu8GrEVrmedve3ikd3qVbU84MB-W8bYELALvIQIVYEI3O0tqKMFNt3pYdWPGce0gI47AoyGw2EvbV8s0FQbUclQSk86rIQ7d-R53zAJbwGgeBqAKABHSoCngQWMDIJgyHwIhSAoKhkHF4xq6FIA) which works, but requires really digging into the Plotly object. 

The key points are:
- Use a FigureWidget to generate the plot so that you can register the widget
- The selected data is stored as a trace in `scatterplot.data[0]`
- Plotly only allows access to the selected data using a call back, so the best approach is to write a function which returns the data as a `reactive.Value`
```
def plotly_selection(trace):
    indices = reactive.Value([])
    def on_selection(trace, points, selector):
        indices.set(points.point_inds)
    trace.on_selection(on_selection)
    return indices
```

Once you have it as a reactive Value you can call it with `points = plotly_selection(scatterplot.data[0])` and then use the `points` object as you would any other reactive value. 

Overall this is quite awkward and reinforces why we need #282 which could follow our existing API for point selection.

title: Reactive problem when using ui.panel_conditional
description:
In some situations, when a ui.panel_conditional has its condition verified, it will trigger unwanted reactivity.

Here is an example :

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import time
from pathlib import Path

from shiny import App, render, ui, reactive

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_radio_buttons("command_choice", "Choose a command", choices=["Option 1", "Option 2"]),

    ui.input_action_button("compute_button", "COMPUTE"),

    ui.panel_conditional(
        "input.command_choice == 'Option 1'",
        ui.output_text("output_text_1")),

    ui.panel_conditional(
        "input.command_choice == 'Option 2'",
        ui.output_text("output_text_2")),
)


def server(input, output, session):

    @output
    @render.text
    @reactive.event(input.compute_button)
    def output_text_1():
        if input.command_choice() == "Option 1":
            message = ui.modal(
                ui.HTML(
                    'output_text_1 is loading...'),
                footer=None,
                easy_close=False,
                fade=True
            )
            ui.modal_show(message)
            time.sleep(2)
            ui.modal_remove()
            return "Result from option 1"

    @output
    @render.text
    @reactive.event(input.compute_button)
    def output_text_2():
        if input.command_choice() == "Option 2":
            message = ui.modal(
                ui.HTML(
                    'output_text_2 is loading...'),
                footer=None,
                easy_close=False,
                fade=True
            )
            ui.modal_show(message)
            time.sleep(2)
            ui.modal_remove()
            return "Result from option 2"

www_dir = Path(__file__).parent / "www"
app = App(app_ui, server, static_assets=www_dir)
```

In this small example, if you click once on the COMPUTE button, then change the radio button selection, you will see that it executes the two `output_text` functions. This is not expected as both functions have a `@reactive.event(input.compute_button)` decorator.

title: Awkward usage for `layout_column_wrap`
description:
The signature for `layout_column_wrap` is this:

```python
def layout_column_wrap(
    width: Optional[CssUnit],
    *args: TagChild | TagAttrs,
    fixed_width: bool = False,
    heights_equal: Literal["all", "row"] = "all",
    fill: bool = True,
    fillable: bool = True,
    height: Optional[CssUnit] = None,
    height_mobile: Optional[CssUnit] = None,
    gap: Optional[CssUnit] = None,
    class_: Optional[str] = None,
    **kwargs: TagAttrValue,
) -> Tag:
```

This makes for kind of awkward usage. Because `width` comes before `*args`, it can _never_ be named when the function is called (assuming you are passing in some `*args`, which you would always want to do). For example:

```python
# These two don't work
layout_column_wrap(width="200px", "Hello", "world")
layout_column_wrap("Hello", "world", width="200px")

# This works
layout_column_wrap("200px", "Hello", "world")
```


On the other hand, `height` _must always_ be named, and come after the `*args`. So if you want to specify both the width and height, you'd have to do this, which is awkward:

```python
layout_column_wrap(1/2, "Hello", "world", height="300px")
```


Another awkward thing is that if you want to set `width` to `None`, you must call the function like this:

```python
layout_column_wrap(None, "Hello", "world")
```

title: Enable standard python logging
description:
In closed issue #305, @jcheng5 advised against using standard python logging (see below). He comments that "we need to fix up our logging to use `logging` everywhere". Has this been done, can we now use standard logging? If not, perhaps we should open this as an issue so it can be prioritized and tracked. Sorry if this is already in process or done. Thanks!

             OK, I missed the fact that you were calling `logging.basicConfig`. I'd stop doing that for now--we need to fix up our logging to use `logging` everywhere, but for now you should just do this instead, as early as possible:

```python
import sys
logfile = open('myapp.log', 'a', 1)
sys.stdout = logfile
sys.stderr = logfile
```

title: `x.ui.layout_column_wrap` width API
description:
The current documentation for this function says that it takes a fractional width between 0-1, but it actually seems to require the following:
1) Between 0.05-1
2) Divides 1 into equal portions with no remainder

I think the current API is confusing because we're really asking the user to provide an integer of the number of divisions, but asking for the reciprocal of that number. This fractional expectation makes the user think that any fraction should work, but it doesn't and produces really confusing cases. For example `0.3333333333333333` is a valid width but `0.333333333333333` is not because three times the former rounds to `1`, while the latter does not.

A couple of things which might help:

1) If width is omitted it should evenly divide the number of children 
2a) User should supply number of divisions instead of the fraction
2b) Allow both and take the reciprocal of numbers greater than 1

title: Remove `session` argument from methods that utilize `require_active_session()`
description:
Having the `session` is good for resolving the correct DOM `id` (such as when in modules), and for sending messages to the browser.

However, some update methods to not utilize the session being sent in: 
* https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/0bc5ad07bac8dd418d27a848f0234ef6d79a2150/shiny/ui/_input_update.py#L226
* https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/0bc5ad07bac8dd418d27a848f0234ef6d79a2150/shiny/ui/_input_update.py#L278

In addition, the session object is something that users shouldn't really be setting.


--------------------------

Proposal:
* Remove `session` from methods whose API has `session` for context only
	* Ex: `update_*()` methods, `notification_{show,remove}()`, etc.
* Internally use `session = require_active_session(None)` to retrieve the session
* Show examples of using `with shiny.session.session_context(session=):` to set the context. Such as in an app where a button updates two modules's checkbox group choices. 

Doing this would naturally resolve the two situations above and make the API cleaner.

title: Full Bootstrap 5
description:
The included bootstrap css and js seem to be missing a bit of bootstrap functionality. 

For example, a striped bootstrap table where certain columns / rows have a background color should be striped with different shades of that background color. This works with CDN bootstrap, but not the included bootstrap css. The `mixins` directory and its `.scss` files don't get generated  / linked. (In this case, that's `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.0/scss/mixins/_table-variants.scss`)

I can hotwire in the CDN bootstrap with `ui.tags.script()` and `ui.tags.link` in a `ui.head_content()` block, but then I have bootstrap conflicts and it only works if I delete the node for the local bootstrap with a Web Inspector in Safari. _Then_ my striped tables look right…

Can we either include all of Bootstrap 5 or have some hook to disable the local CSS/JS (either altogether so one can manually link to CDN or specifically in favor of the one on the CDN instead?)

title: Allow for session "on flush" and "on flushed" callbacks to be async
description:
Pro: 
* You can call `session.send_custom_message()` which is an await-able method in an "on flush" callback.

Cons: 
* The callbacks are not done within the same tick if there is a truly await-able method.
* The next callback is started after the previous callback finishes, which could be a while. 
	* Is there a way to "promise all" and launch all callbacks within the same start tick?

title: 0.5.0: sidebar layout broken, along with some other missing bslib styling
description:
Some of the bslib styling previously embedded into `bootstrap.min.css` was relocated between releases 0.4.0 and 0.5.0, but it isn't loaded into the web page.

Example - in 0.4.0 `.bslib-sidebar-layout` has styling applied to it in `bootstrap.min.js`, but as of 0.5.0, in the repo this styling was removed and relocated to `/shiny/www/shared/_x/bslib/components/sidebar/sidebar.css`, and this file is not currently being loaded in the page.  This produces a visibly different layout in the following minimal example when switching between `pip install shiny==0.4.0` and `pip install shiny==0.5.0`:
```
from shiny import App, ui

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.layout_sidebar(
        ui.panel_sidebar('Sidebar content'),
        ui.panel_main('Main content')
    )
)

app = App(app_ui, None)
```

Not super familiar with the codebase, so I'm not sure where this is controlled or what the best resolution is.  Thanks!

title: Input for tabular data?
description:
I'm just scratching the surface of Shiny, so my question might have an obvious answer, but I wasn't able to answer it based on the [UI inputs API](https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/#ui-inputs).

Is there a canonical way to create a tabular input area where the user can directly paste data copied from a spreadsheet application? I'm thinking of something like [streamlit.data_editor()](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/api-reference/data/st.data_editor).

In my experience, there are countless ways in which users mess up when converting spreadsheets to comma- or tab-delimited data before pasting the result in a regular [input_text_area()](https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/ui.input_text_area.html#shiny.ui.input_text_area). An input for tabular data, even returning a list of lists of `str`, would be incredibly useful.

1) Add a `@render.plotly` decorator which did a better job at rendering plotly than our current implementation (see #620). This could have a `streaming` or `in_place` argument to trigger the streaming behaviour.
2) Investigate whether something similar would work for matplotlib plots

title: Plotly widget sizing issue within rows
description:
I am experiencing an issue with the sizing of Plotly widgets when placed within rows in Shiny for Python. Currently, when I create a row using ui.row() and include a Plotly widget, the widget automatically adjusts its size to fit the default row height. However, this default height is too small for the Plotly widget, resulting in a suboptimal display.

**Steps to reproduce:**
Create a new Shiny for Python application.
Add the following code snippet to your application:

```
ui.row(
  ui.column(
    12,
    ui.div(
      {"class": "app-col"},
      output_widget("plot_widget"),
    ),
  ),
)
```

Replace output_widget("plot_widget") with the appropriate code for your Plotly widget.
Run the application and observe the size of the Plotly widget within the row.
Expected behavior:
The Plotly widget should adjust its size to fit the available space within the row, ensuring optimal display and readability.

**Actual behavior:**
The Plotly widget automatically sizes itself to the default row height, which is too small, resulting in a cramped and difficult-to-read visualization.

**Additional information:**
I have tested this issue on multiple browsers, and the behavior is consistent.

**Environment:**
Python version: 3.8.13
ipydatagrid version: 1.1.16
ipywidgets version: 8.0.6
Other relevant libraries and their versions: pandas=2.0.2
Browser: Safari and Microsoft Edge


Thank you!

title: Type check fails with recent versions of pyright
description:
Starting with pyright 1.1.313 (I think), we've started getting errors like this:


```
  /Users/winston/Projects/py-shiny/shiny/ui/_bootstrap.py:76:43 - error: Argument of type "TagAttrValue" cannot be assigned to parameter "_add_ws" of type "bool" in function "div"
    Type "TagAttrValue" cannot be assigned to type "bool"
      "float" is incompatible with "bool" (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```

https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/f29d8a20166e4e1545170d35ef05c80385136802/shiny/ui/_bootstrap.py#L47-L76

The problem is that the `**kwargs` have type `TagAttrValue`, but when it passes them along to `div()`, they may encompass the `_add_ws` parameter, which has type `bool`.

Some potentially useful references:
* https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/issues/5351
* https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/discussions/5231
* https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/issues/5358

title: `bind_fill_role()`, `as_fillable_container()`, and `as_fill_item()` modify their inputs
description:
I don't think this is something we need to address immediately, but I'm filing it here so that we remember to come back to it. The functions `bind_fill_role()`, `as_fillable_container()`, and `as_fill_item()` mutate the objects that are passed into them. Here's an example of how this could cause confusing behavior: ```py from shiny import ui from shiny.experimental.ui._fill import bind_fill_role x = ui.div() y = bind_fill_role( x, item=True ) y.append("Hello") y #>
Hello
# We thought we were just modifying y, but we modified x as well: x #>
Hello
``` One possible solution that @schloerke and I discussed is to bundle and always include the fill.css file, so that no HTML dependency object is needed, and then simply include the attributes. Here are some possibilities of what the API could look like: ```py # Use literal class names ui.div("Hello", class_="html-fill-item") # Use class name from a variable ui.div("Hello", class_=ui.FILL_ITEM_CLASS) # Use function that returns class attributes ui.div("Hello", fill_item_attrs()) ```

title: Dynamic Creation of Tabs
Inconsistent Popup Window Placement When Using ipydatagrid with pyshiny 0.3.3
description:
### **Issue Description:**
I encountered unexpected behavior while attempting to embed an interactive table using ipydatagrid. Specifically, when utilizing pyshiny 0.3.3 and ipywidgets to embed an ipydatagrid widget on my website, the table renders correctly. However, an issue arises when attempting to interact with the table, such as sorting columns or performing other actions. The window that displays the available options appears at the bottom of the site page instead of directly adjacent to the datagrid widget.

### **Steps to Reproduce:**

1. Install pyshiny version 0.3.3.
2. Set up a website with ipywidgets support.
3. Embed an ipydatagrid widget within the website.
4. Attempt to interact with the embedded datagrid by sorting a column or performing other actions.
5. Observe that the window displaying options appears at the bottom of the site page instead of next to the datagrid widget.

```
import numpy as np
from shiny import ui, module
from shinywidgets import render_widget, output_widget
import pandas as pd
from ipydatagrid import DataGrid

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['x'] = np.random.normal(0, 1, 10)
df['y'] = np.random.normal(0, 1, 10)

@module.ui
def bins_ui():
    return ui.tags.div(
        ui.panel_title("Rendering Table using ipydatagrid"),
            ui.panel_main(
                output_widget("table"),
            ),
        )

@module.server
def bins_server(input, output, session):
    @output
    @render_widget
    def table():
        global df
        grid = DataGrid(df)
        return grid
```


### **Expected Behavior:**
When interacting with the ipydatagrid widget embedded using pyshiny 0.3.3 and ipywidgets, the window displaying available options should appear adjacent to the datagrid widget.

### **Actual Behavior:**
Currently, when attempting to sort columns or perform other actions on the ipydatagrid widget, the window that should display options appears at the bottom of the site page rather than next to the datagrid widget.

### **Additional Information:**
Python version: 3.8.13
ipydatagrid version: 1.1.16
ipywidgets version: 8.0.6
Other relevant libraries and their versions: pandas=2.0.2
Browser: Safari and Microsoft Edge

![screenshot](https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/assets/85912927/223f4083-4933-4823-a0d1-681a2834ecd0)

I click at 1, but the popup occurs at 2.

title: Improve module id errors
description:
From a documentation issue:

"In the docs for modules (https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/docs/workflow-modules.html) it's not explicitly documented that the first argument for the id must be added silently. (Not sure I'm describing this correctly, or in the most elegant way.)

What I mean is that the function definition in the UI and server has one argument:

def counter_ui(label: str = "Increment counter"):
But when you call this function, you must prepend the ID, like this:

counter_ui("counter1", "Counter 1"),
So, when I say add the id silently, I refer to counter1 in this example. If you forget to do this, you get all kinds of very strange, non-descriptive errors."

I doubt we can solve this with documentation, so we should make the function error more gracefully.

title: Improve release workflow
description:
Currently, to make a release to PyPI, we:

- Tag a commit and push
- Make a GitHub release

The GitHub Action workflow does the rest This is pretty simple, but there is a problem: if the release fails for some reason, like if it has trouble uploading to PyPI, or if there's some bug in the PyPI publishing script (which can happen because it's not used very often) then the "release" is not actually a release, and we need to go back, delete the GitHub Release and the tag.

It would be nice if we could push a branch with a certain prefix, like `release-v1.0.0`, and the action would attempt publishing to PyPI, and then if successful it would tag it and create a GitHub Release. It could also delete the branch.

title: @render.txt works differently than expected compared to R
Consider alternative name for "modules"
description:
We chose the name "modules" for two main reasons:

1) It's the same as the R term which makes transitioning a bit easier
2) Shiny modules are pretty similar to generic Python modules so it made sense to use the name

The name does seem to create confusion in some users and is difficult to explain. For example I ended up saying: "the Shiny `module_ui` function is in Shiny's UI module". 

According to chatGPT the most common term for this is "Component" so maybe we should go with `@component.ui` and `@component.server`.

Web Framework | Reusable Elements
-- | --
React | Components
Angular | Components
Vue.js | Components
Ember.js | Components
Backbone.js | Views or Templates
Meteor.js | Templates or Components
Express.js | Middleware or Router Middleware
Next.js | Components
Svelte | Components
Preact | Components
Django | Templates or Views
Dash | Components
Streamlit | Components or Widgets

title: Why not a generic `@render` decorator?
description:

In some of my test apps, my server function has more lines of decorators than lines of code in the functions.

title: Markdown UI with Shiny objects
description:
I know this has come up in various forms, from https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/issues/518 to flexdashboards. But it would really be great if I could lay out my shiny UI with markdown so that I can more quickly get started with an app. 

To get a sense of what this could feel like, I did a prototype rewriting the "Hello Shiny" example with markdown. I wrote a function with a couple of regular expressions to substitute in shiny.ui inputs and outputs. I used `{}` for inline values, as quarto does (at least in some contexts), and I chose `${{ }}` to enclose Python code that returns shiny.ui tags. (The hugo and quarto shortcode `{{< >}}` could have worked but the convention there isn't literal code you eval so it wasn't a direct fit, and `{python}` triple-backtick code blocks like quarto uses seemed misleading. But I'm not proposing a complete design, just making something that runs for illustrative purposes.)

In the end, the UI looked like 

```
## Hello Shiny!

${{ ui.input_slider("n", "N", 0, 100, 20) }}

`n * 2` is {n2}
```

Shinylive example [here](https://shinylive.io/py/editor/#-AsHkwMoqKAsEWIYWHbbGUTibDGcQWaxzQKENBwKwijDY--1aJQAhfGhSBWrwAAEI6iQEE-GxgMG-Rq4EMd3swcOsvBploogwX4XUd+noHQI0FCzRntCj9Qg8YWswEGZkgA). 

To me, something like this seems like it would really help with laying out basic UIs or parts of UIs, and if you went the whole flexdashboard direction, you could specify your whole UI in markdown, just putting your various `ui.input_*()` and `ui.output_*()` where they should go.

title: Improvement Suggestion: Pythonic API for pyshiny
description:
Hello PyShiny team,

Firstly, I'd like to express my appreciation for your effort in porting RShiny to Python.

However, I see that the current design of PyShiny's API is very similar to its R counterpart, which might be comfortable for R users transitioning to Python, but it's somewhat unintuitive for Python developers.

For instance, I noticed that the library requires functions/variables to be passed as strings. While this might be a common pattern in R, it's not the way Python developers typically work. Similarly with defining functions inside functions that are not just ad-hoc helper functions, I'd rather see them as methods.

For instance I took the [streamlit-shiny-dash](https://github.com/rstudio/streamlit-shiny-dash/blob/main/shiny-app.py) example.
The more pythonic API might look like that:

```python
from shiny import App, UI, Reactive, Render
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import ggplot, aes, theme_bw, geom_point, scale_x_log10, scale_y_log10, geom_histogram


class MyAppUI(UI):
    def __init__(self):
        self.sample_slider = self.input_slider("Sample Size", 0, 1, value = 0.1)
        self.log_checkbox = self.input_checkbox("Log Scale")

        # placeholders for the elements which will be dynamically updated
        self.first_taxi_id_text = self.output_text()
        self.tip_plot = self.output_plot()
        self.amount_histogram = self.output_plot()

        sidebar = self.panel_sidebar(self.sample_slider, self.log_checkbox)
        main_panel = self.panel_main(self.h3(self.first_taxi_id_text), self.tip_plot, self.amount_histogram)

        self.layout = self.page_fluid(self.layout_sidebar(sidebar, main_panel))

class MyAppServer:
    def __init__(self, ui: MyAppUI):
        self.ui = ui
        dat = Reactive(self.load_data)
        sampled_dat = Reactive(self.sample_data, dat, self.ui.sample_slider)

        # Assign the output of the reactive functions to the UI placeholders
        self.ui.first_taxi_id_text.set_render_function(Render.text(self.first_taxi_id, sampled_dat))
        self.ui.tip_plot.set_render_function(Render.plot(self.create_tip_plot, sampled_dat, self.ui.log_checkbox))
        self.ui.amount_histogram.set_render_function(Render.plot(self.create_amount_histogram, sampled_dat))

    def load_data(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        df = pd.read_csv('nyc-taxi.csv')
        return df

    def sample_data(self, df: pd.DataFrame, fraction: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
        return df.copy().sample(frac=fraction)

    def first_taxi_id(self, df: pd.DataFrame) -> str:
        return f'First taxi ID: {df["taxi_id"].iloc[0]}'

    def create_tip_plot(self, df: pd.DataFrame, log_scale: bool) -> ggplot.ggplot:
        plot = (ggplot(df, aes('tip_amount', 'total_amount')) + geom_point() + theme_bw())
        if log_scale:
            plot = (plot + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10())
        return plot

    def create_amount_histogram(self, df: pd.DataFrame) -> ggplot.ggplot:
        plot = (ggplot(df, aes(x='total_amount')) + geom_histogram() + theme_bw())
        return plot

class MyApp(App):
    def __init__(self):
        self.ui = MyAppUI()
        self.server = MyAppServer(self.ui)
        super().__init__(self.ui.layout, self.server)

app = MyApp()
```

I understand that this would involve a significant refactor of the current design and I don't want to argue this is the best API by any means (it might even not work due to some error that I made).
However, I genuinely believe a discussion around the more pythonic API could be very beneficial as it could improve the adoption of PyShiny in the Python community, and provide a better user experience for Python developers.

I would love to open this for discussion and hear the thoughts of others. 

Best

title: Add option to send text input only after pressing return key
description:
Ask: Please consider adding an option to input_text_input and input_text_area_input to only send new input information after the user presses the return key. Below links to the bindings I have used with R-shiny. 

Why: My apps ask users to input filters, arguments, and commands. This will throw errors if the user input is not complete. Adding an input_action_button works only for the first text entry. Once the action button has been pushed, any changes to the user text input are immediately sent for processing.

I have tested the js scripts linked below with the input_text_area function below and it works. All that should be needed is to (1) source the js and (2) append "returnTextArea" to the classes list.

Thank you for your consideration.

https://github.com/radiant-rstats/radiant.data/blob/master/inst/app/www/js/returnTextAreaBinding.js

https://github.com/radiant-rstats/radiant.data/blob/master/inst/app/www/js/returnTextInputBinding.js

```python
def input_return_text_area(
    id,
    label,
    value="",
    rows=1,
    placeholder="",
    resize="vertical",
    autocomplete=False,
    spellcheck=False,
):
    classes = ["form-control", "returnTextArea"]
    area = tags.textarea(
        value,
        id=id,
        class_=" ".join(classes),
        style=css(width="100%", height=None, resize=resize),
        placeholder=placeholder,
        rows=rows,
        cols=None,
        autocomplete=autocomplete,
        spellcheck=spellcheck,
    )

    def shiny_input_label(id, label=None):
        cls = "control-label" + ("" if label else " shiny-label-null")
        return tags.label(label, class_=cls, id=id + "-label", for_=id)

    return div(
        shiny_input_label(id, label),
        area,
        None,
        class_="form-group shiny-input-container",
        style=css(width="100%"),
    )
```

title: Updated nav/navset API names
description:
In rstudio/bslib#546, we renamed many of the `nav_*()` and `navset_*()` functions in the R API. Many of these now align with the Python naming, but there are some notable differences. Here's a summary table:

| bslib (new) | Python (current) | Changes? |
|:--|:--|:-:|
| `nav_panel()` | [ui.nav](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.nav.html) | 👀 |
| `nav_panel_hidden()` | ui.nav_content | 👀 ❗ |
| `navset_tab()` | [ui.navset_tab](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.navset_tab.html) | |
| `navset_pill()` | [ui.navset_pill](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.navset_pill.html) |
| `navset_pill_list()` | [ui.navset_pill_list](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.navset_pill_list.html) | |
| `navset_hidden()` | ui.navset_hidden | ❗ |
| `navset_bar()` | ui.navset_bar | ❗ |
| `navset_card_tab()` | [ui.navset_tab_card](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.navset_tab_card.html) | 👀 |
| `navset_card_pill()` | [ui.navset_pill_card](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.navset_pill_card.html) | 👀 |

👀 new R name is different from current Python
❗ not in API refs

Note that this research also uncovered that `ui.navset_bar` and `ui.navset_tab_card` are exported but don't appear in [the API reference](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api).

title: Add highlight.js for syntax highlighting
description:
(Reframing the issue based on the discussion)

Syntax highlighting with highlight.js will work with the code blocks that `ui.markdown()` produces, or any `<pre><code>` block. It requires:

* A JS file
* A CSS file, which varies by theme
* A script tag to call `highlightAll()` on the page

We probably want to set the theme globally, like with bootswatch: the highlight.js interface does not seem to be set up to apply different style to parts of the page, nor does that seem worth the effort to support. 

We need every `ui.markdown()` to call `highlightAll()`, like @wch shows below, so that dynamically generated UI gets updated. 

If I understand correctly then, we either need to always add the highlight.js JS code, or only add the highlightAll call if highlight.js has been added to the page, or otherwise shim the Shiny JS so that `hljs.highlightAll();` doesn't error if it is invoked in a markdown block but someone hasn't added highlighting/theming to the page.

title: ui.update_slider fails with datetime slider, if value is specified
description:
Hello,

I ran into the issue that updating a datetime slider fails when the value is specified.
The application stops with the following error message : 

```
_send_error_response: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable
INFO:     connection closed
```

In the following simple example, the application will stop when clicking the "Update Slider" button.
When commenting out the value property (line 13 of the example), the slider is updated without issue.

```
import shiny
from shiny import *
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

print(shiny.__version__)

app_ui = ui.page_bootstrap(
    ui.h2("Hello Shiny!"),
    ui.panel_well(
        ui.input_slider("in_timerange", "Timerange Slider",
                min=datetime.now() - timedelta(days=1),
                max=datetime.now(),
                value=[datetime.now() - timedelta(days=1), datetime.now()],
                time_format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
                step=3600,
                width="90%"
        ),
        class_="mx-5"
    ),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("txt"),
    ui.input_action_button("in_update_slider", "Update Slider")
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @output
    @render.text
    def txt():
        return input.in_timerange()

    @reactive.Effect
    @reactive.event(input.in_update_slider)
    def update_slider():
        ui.update_slider(
            "in_timerange",
            min=datetime.now() - timedelta(days=10),
            max=datetime.now(),
            # commenting out the value makes the example work
            value=(datetime.now() - timedelta(days=5), datetime.now() - timedelta(days=1)),
            time_format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
            step=3600
        )

app = App(app_ui, server)

def main():
    run_app(app)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The error occurs in the function  _send_message, on line 609 of file shiy/session/_session.py. The message property still contains a datetime value, which cannot be serialized.

``` 
    async def _send_message(self, message: dict[str, object]) -> None:
        message_str: str = json.dumps(message) + "\n"
```

I've noticed that the min and max properties are converted to numeric values, but the value is kept untouched (function update_slider of file shiny/ui/_input_update.py, lines 719 - 799, especially lines 778 - 799)

I think this can be solved by modifying the value with something like : 

```
value = tuple((_as_numeric(val) for val in value)) if isinstance(value, tuple) else _as_numeric(val)
```

before putting it into the msg dict. 
Unfortunately, it's no solution to pass numeric datetime values (with timestamp()), because the data type is used to calculate the data_type property of the slider.

I also noticed that the ui.update_slider expects a **Optional[SliderValueArg | tuple[SliderValueArg, SliderValueArg]]**, while the function ui.input_slider expects a **SliderValueArg | Iterable[SliderValueArg]**. This is a little confusing, and the same argument type would be preferable.

Kind Regards

Bart

title: Add include_* for static content
description: We took `include_html` out of https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/pull/127 because it seems like this needs a different strategy. There are a few use cases that we want to consider: - Include HTML in iframe (which is what's implemented below) - Include inline HTML - Include Markdown like (`shiny::includeMarkdown()`) - Maybe `include_qmd` to render a quarto document and include it as an HTML file? The old implementation for reference. ``` @add_example() def include_html( path: str, *, method: Literal["link", "link_files"] = "link", attrs: TagAttrs = {}, ) -> Tag: """ Include an HTML file Parameters ---------- path A path to an HTML file. method One of the following: * ``"link"``: Link to the CSS file via a :func:`~ui.tags.link` tag. * ``"link_files"``: Same as ``"link"``, but also allow for the HTML file to request other files within ``path``'s immediate parent directory (e.g., include an HTML ```` that points to another local file). This isn't the default behavior because you should **be careful not to include files in the same directory as ``path`` that contain sensitive information**. A good general rule of thumb to follow is to have ``path`` be located in a subdirectory of the app directory. For example, if the app's source is located at ``/app/app.py``, then ``path`` should be somewhere like ``/app/html/index.html`` (and all the other relevant accompanying 'safe' files should be located under ``/app/html/``). attrs Additional attributes to add to the :func:`~ui.tags.iframe` tag. Returns ------- A :func:`~ui.tags.iframe` tag. Note ---- For safety reasons, this function includes the HTML file as a :func:`~ui.tags.iframe`, which means it's 'isolated' from the rest of the parent document. If instead, you don't want to isolate (meaning, among other things, you want the HTML inherit CSS styles from the parent document), you can do something like this: .. code-block:: python from shiny import ui with open("custom.html", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: custom_html = ui.HTML(f.read()) app_ui = ui.page_fluid(..., custom_html, ...) See also -------- ~ui.tags.iframe ~ui.HTML ~include_javascript ~include_css """ include_files = method == "link_files" path_dest, hash = maybe_copy_files(path, include_files) dep, src = create_include_dependency( "include-html-" + hash, path_dest, include_files ) default_attrs: TagAttrs = { "src": src, "scrolling": "no", "seamless": "seamless", "frameBorder": "0", } return tags.iframe(default_attrs, dep, **attrs) ```

title: Pooling database connections
description:
This is related to:
- Usage of global variables ([this](https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/issues/469) issue)
- Alternatively: how to run `shiny.App` with arbitrary parameters passed onto `app_server`.

---

As as user of R Shiny, I’ve been using in the past the package `pool` , both in a single file (as specified [here](https://shiny.posit.co/r/articles/build/pool-basics/)) and setting the pool in a `global.R` file.

The intention was to instantiate a connection pool per application, and then let each R session use a connection from this pool. It worked as expected, because as specified [here](https://shiny.posit.co/r/articles/improve/scoping/), objects in `global.R` are “loaded into the global environment of the R session; all R code in a Shiny app is run in the global environment or a child of it”.

Back to Python: in [issue 469](https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/issues/469) it was specified that Shiny Python does not have an equivalent mechanism to `global.R`. Indeed I’ve tried several approaches to instantiate a pool connection (I am using [MongoDB](https://pymongo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/pymongo/pool.html), but it could also be [postgres](https://medium.com/@dipan.saha/python-connection-pooling-a72356a04e53#:~:text=Here%20are%20some%20best%20practices%20to%20keep%20in,...%205%20Be%20mindful%20of%20connection%20timeouts.%20)) and use it inside server code, but nothing seems to work. And if I have code like:

```
def run_app():
    app = App(app_ui, app_server)
    app.run()
```
`app_server`, of type `Callable[[Inputs, Outputs, Session], None]`, does not accept any additional, arbitrary inputs.

If `app_server` could behave like the server side of a module, allowing additional parameters, the code could perhaps look like:
```
def run_app():
   postgres_pool = psycopg2.pool.SimpleConnectionPool(
      # arguments to connect ...
   )

   app = App(app_ui, app_server(connection_pool=postgres_pool))
   app.run()
```

And `connection_pool.getconn()` would be executed inside the `app_server` code.

Is there currently a way to achieve this behaviour pooling connections?

Thanks in advance.

title: Clarify use of global variables
description:
Is there a recommended approach to setting global variables that can be used a) in the application code and b) as parameters to `run_app`?

In R, we would typically set up global variables/options in `R/global.R`, e.g.,

```
# R/global.R
options(shiny.host = "0.0.0.0", shiny.port = "8888")
```

When `shiny::runApp` is called, `R/global.R` is sourced automatically, and the app is therefore served at port 8888.

In Python, the closest equivalent design that I can figure out is to create files for global variables and for calling `run_app`, e.g.,

```
# globals.py
port = 8888
app_title = "Hello world"
```

```
# app.py
from shiny import App, ui
from globals import app_title
app_ui = ui.page_fluid(ui.h1(app_title))
app = App(app_ui, None)
```

```
# run.py
from shiny import run_app
from globals import port
run_app(port=port)
```

```
# bash
python run.py
```

Is this an appropriate architecture for defining global variables/options to pass to py-shiny apps? Is there a better way, and if so, is that documented anywhere? Thanks!

title: Security: DataTables.net prototype pollution
description:
Shiny packages a rather old version of DataTables (1.10.5, from 2015, https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/main/shiny/www/shared/datatables/js/jquery.dataTables.min.js). This version has a prototype pollution vulnerability. In Sonatype's words:

> The datatables.net package is vulnerable to Prototype Pollution. The setData function in jquery.dataTables.js fails to protect prototype attributes when objects are created during the application's execution. A remote attacker can exploit this to modify the behavior of object prototypes which, depending on their use in the application, may result in a Denial of Service (DoS), Remote Code Execution (RCE), or other unexpected execution flow.

This vulnerability was apparently [fixed](https://github.com/DataTables/Dist-DataTables/commit/e2e19eac7e5a6f140d7eefca5c7deba165b357eb) in DataTables 1.10.13.

There is an equivalent, open issue in the R version of Shiny here: https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/issues/3627. That specific case is complicated by the fact that `DT::renderDT` is slowly superseding `shiny::renderDataTable`, though they are not always compatible. 

Can I suggest that, given py-shiny is in a pre-1.x release phase, DataTables is updated to a more recent version, e.g., 1.13.x? It's not totally clear to me that this vulnerability is exploitable in a py-shiny app, but I think it makes sense to use a more up-to-date version of DataTables anyway.

Happy to contribute a MR for this, let me know if that would be useful. Thanks

title: Problems with editable installs and setuptools >=64
description:
With Python 3.11.3, I installed Shiny in a venv for another project, with `pip install -e ../py-shiny`, but when I did this, the new project couldn't find the `py.typed` file.

I'm not 100% sure, but I believe that this is because setuptools >=64 uses a new mechanism instead of `egg-link`.
See:

- https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/13392#issuecomment-1212727421
- https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/3518

Apparently one can also install with `strict` mode (https://setuptools.pypa.io/en/latest/userguide/development_mode.html#strict-editable-installs):

```
pip install -e ../py-shiny --config-settings editable_mode=strict
```

I tried this with py-shiny, and it resulted in the JS and CSS web assets not being available when running an app. So we'll probably want to fix it in that case.


What _does_ work for now is to use `compat` mode:

```
pip install -e ../py-shiny --config-settings editable_mode=compat
```

title: Brushing dates in shinylive results in error
description:
When brushing dates in shinylive, it results in this error:

```
Error: cannot astype a datetimelike from [datetime64[ns, UTC]] to [int32]
```

The problem is this line:
https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/44e6e8c9858bc5f6d37277fa578c4472ff4fcfee/shiny/plotutils.py#L361

Specifically, it tries to convert the datetime to an `int`. On most computers, that is an `int64`, but in Pyodide, it's an `int32`.

Small reproducible example. First, this is what happens when converting explicitly to `int64` and `int32`:

```py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(np.datetime64('2005-01-03 14:30:00.000000000'))

s.astype("int64")
#> 0    1104762600000000000
#> dtype: int64

s.astype("int32")
#> TypeError: cannot astype a datetimelike from [datetime64[ns]] to [int32]
```


The behavior of `int` conversion differs:

```
# M1 Mac
s.astype("int")
#> 0    1104762600000000000
#> dtype: int64


# Shinylive/Pyodide
s.astype("int")
#> TypeError: cannot astype a datetimelike from [datetime64[ns]] to [int32]
```

This is happening because Pyodide is 32 bit (perhaps because wasm is 32 bit?).

title: `reactive.Effect` should warn if function returns a value
description:
For example, if a user writes this:

```py
@reactive.Effect
def foo():
  return 123
```

It will run and the user will not receive any indication that the code is probably not doing what they expect. (It will be flagged by a static type checker like pyright, but many users don't use them.)

This should raise an informative warning. (And come to think of it, we should do that in R as well. But now that I think about it again, we can't tell in R if a function just returned a value because it happened to be the last expression when running the function, or if the function was really intended to return the value, so we can't add this check in R.)

title: Accessing an empty reactive Value raises a SilentException
description:
Hi,

I was trying to implement a lazy loading mechanism. 
The data is defined as a reactive.Value, but is initially not initialized.
The data is loaded in a reactive Effect, that is fired when some other event is occurring (e.g. a button click, a nav item becoming active). The reactive Effect needs to check if the reactive Value is empty, and if so, it loads the required data and sets the reactive Value. Otherwise, it does nothing.
To get the current value of the reactive Value, I'm using a **with isolate** block. However, this block is raising a SilentException, and the next steps (the data load) never happens.
This is not limited to an isolate block. When used in an output function, the function stops when the empty reactive value is encountered.

Here's a simple example : 

```
from shiny import *

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.h2("Lazy Load Demo"),
    ui.input_action_button("in_load", "Load Data"),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("out_data", placeholder=True),
    ui.input_text("in_text", "Some text"),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("out_text", placeholder=True),
)


def server(input, output, session):

    data = reactive.Value()
    # workaround:
    # data = reactive.Value(False) or reactive.Value(pd.DataFrame())

    @reactive.Effect
    def load_data():
        """
        Load data on demand. But only load it once.
        If the data has been loaded before, do not reload
        """
        req(input.in_load())

        with reactive.isolate():
            # check if data is loaded. Avoid dependency with the reactive value
            # if using an initialized reactive.Value, the check may be different, e.g.
            # loaded = data()
            loaded = data() is not None

        # This is never executed:
        if loaded:
            print("data already loaded, skipping")
        else:
            print("loading data, skipping")
            data.set("Simulate")


    @output
    @render.text
    def out_data():
        """
        Also in the output function, calling the non-initialized reactive Value results in a SilentException.

        """
        # req(data())

        print("Rendering output")
        # This is never executed:
        print(data())
        print("data printed")

        return data()

    @output
    @render.text
    def out_text():
        return input.in_text()

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

I would expect that an empty reactive Value would simply return None, instead of raising a SilentException.
My workaround for the moment is to initialize the reactive Value with a value, such as False, or pd.DataFrame().

Shiny version : 0.2.9

Kind Regards,

Bart

title: Calling function to start a shiny-for-python app from a jupyter notebook?
description:
It is possible launch an R-shiny app from a jupyter-notebook running an R-kernel. It opens up in a new tab. Could something similar be done for a shiny-for-python app? For example, calling a function or instantiating a class that starts a shiny app.

I was hoping that something like the below might work (but then wrapped in a function) but that returns: `RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop`


```
from shiny import *
from shinywidgets import output_widget, register_widget, reactive_read
import ipyleaflet as L

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_slider("zoom", "Map zoom level", value=4, min=1, max=10),
    output_widget("map"),
    ui.output_text("map_bounds"),
)

def server(input, output, session):

    # Initialize and display when the session starts (1)
    map = L.Map(center=(52, 360), zoom=4)
    register_widget("map", map)

    # When the slider changes, update the map's zoom attribute (2)
    @reactive.Effect
    def _():
        map.zoom = input.zoom()

    # When zooming directly on the map, update the slider's value (2 and 3)
    @reactive.Effect
    def _():
        ui.update_slider("zoom", value=reactive_read(map, "zoom"))

    # Everytime the map's bounds change, update the output message (3)
    @output
    @render.text
    def map_bounds():
        b = reactive_read(map, "bounds")
        lat = [b[0][0], b[0][1]]
        lon = [b[1][0], b[1][1]]
        return f"The current latitude is {lat} and longitude is {lon}"

run_app(App(app_ui, server))
```

May be related to https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/issues/303

title: Can we use plotly in Python Shiny?
Nested tabs (navs) sometimes cause output_widget not to render
description:
Hello,

I'm having an issue with a Shiny application with nested navs, and a plotly figure using shinywidgets. Because the issue only (?) occurs when nested navs are involved, I suspect this is a shiny issue, and not a shinywidgets issue.

I have narrowed down the problem to the following sample program.
The app is constructed as a page_navbar, with 2 tabs, "Nav A" and "Nav B".
"Nav A" is built as a navset_tab with two subtabs, "SubNav A" and "SubNav B". "SubNav A" contains a first output_widget, i.e. this is an output_widget on level 2 of the nav tree.
"Nav B" is containing a second output_widget. This is an output_widget on level 1 of the nav tree.

The weird thing is that the first output_widget (level 2) is only displayed if the second output_widget (level 1) exists.
If I comment out the second output_widget, the first one is not rendered.
The second output_widget doesn't even need to be rendered. Just having the output_widget in the ui is enough to be able to render the first one.

Here's a sample program demonstrating the issue (you need to play with comments on the output_widget from Section 2).

```
from shiny import *
from shinywidgets import *

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go

df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(50, 3), index=range(50), columns=["x", "y", "z"])

# App consists of a top navigation bar, with 2 navigation items "Nav A" and "Nav B"
app_ui = ui.page_navbar(
    ui.nav(
        "Nav A",
        # Section 1 : nested navset, with one nav containing an output_widget
        # This only renders correctly if there's an output_widget in the "Nav B" tab
        ui.navset_tab(
            ui.nav("SubNav A",
                   ui.h3("Plotly widget 1"),
                   output_widget("out_plotly_widget1"),
                   ),
            ui.nav("SubNav B")
        ),
    ),
    ui.nav(
        "Nav B",
        # Section 2 : the output_widget must exist for the first output_widget (above) to render
        ui.h3("Plotly widget 2"),
        output_widget("out_plotly_widget2"),
    ),
    ui.nav_control(
        ui.input_select("in_selection", label=None, choices=[1,2,3,4])
    ),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    selected_value = reactive.Value()

    @reactive.Effect
    def _():
        req(input.in_selection())

        selected_value.set(input.in_selection())

    @output
    @render_widget
    def out_plotly_widget1():
        fig = px.scatter(df, x="x", y="y")

        return go.FigureWidget(fig)

    # Only for illustrative reasons.
    # Doesn't make a difference if this rendering function exists or not
    # Can be commented out without any impact
    @output
    @render_widget
    def out_plotly_widget2():
        fig = px.scatter(df, x="y", y="z")

        return go.FigureWidget(fig)

app = App(app_ui, server)

```

So this works : 

- Section 1 + Section 2

This doesn't work : 

- Section 1 ( Section 2 commented out)


In a further test, I also inluded a navset_tab for "Nav B". It appears that it's not enough to have an output widget defined on level 2.
There needs to be a widget on level 1 (dummy or not). 

In the following code snippet, I moved out_plotly_widget_2 one level down, and added a dummy widget in "Nav B".

```
from shiny import *
from shinywidgets import *

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go

df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(50, 3), index=range(50), columns=["x", "y", "z"])

# App consists of a top navigation bar, with 2 navigation items "Nav A" and "Nav B"
app_ui = ui.page_navbar(
    ui.nav(
        "Nav A",
        # Section 1 : nested navset, with one nav containing an output_widget
        # This only renders correctly if there's an output_widget in the "Nav B" tab
        ui.navset_tab(
            ui.nav("SubNav AA",
                   ui.h3("Plotly widget 1"),
                   output_widget("out_plotly_widget1"),
                   ),
            ui.nav("SubNav AB")
        ),
    ),
    ui.nav(
        "Nav B",
        # Section 2 : the output_widget must exist for the first output_widget (above) to render
        ui.navset_tab(
            ui.nav("SubNav BB",
                   ui.h3("Plotly widget 2"),
                   output_widget("out_plotly_widget2"),
                   ),
            ui.nav("SubNav BB")
        ),
        # ui.h3("Dummy widget"),
        output_widget("dummy widget"),
    )
)


def server(input, output, session):
    selected_value = reactive.Value()

    @reactive.Effect
    def _():
        req(input.in_selection())

        selected_value.set(input.in_selection())

    @output
    @render_widget
    def out_plotly_widget1():
        fig = px.scatter(df, x="x", y="y")

        return go.FigureWidget(fig)

    # Only for illustrave reasons.
    # Doesn't make a difference if this rendering function exists or not
    # Can be commented out without any impact
    @output
    @render_widget
    def out_plotly_widget2():
        fig = px.scatter(df, x="y", y="z")

        return go.FigureWidget(fig)

app = App(app_ui, server, debug=True)
```

It doesn't seem to matter where you put the dummy widget (Nav A or Nav B).

So there seems to be a workaround ...

Thanks for having a look.

Bart

description:
I've noticed that the width attribute for certain inputs is not working correctly.
I'm using shiny 0.2.9

It seems to be working for input_text, but not for input_select or input_slider.

Here's an example

```
from shiny import App, render, ui

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.h2("Hello Shiny!"),
    ui.input_text("text_default", "Default text (300px)", "Some text"),
    ui.input_text("text_width", "50% text (ok)", "Some text", width="50%"),

    ui.input_slider("slider_width", "50% Slider (not ok, 300px)", 0, 100, 20, width="50%"),
    ui.panel_well(
        ui.input_text("well_text_default", "Default text (100%)", "Some text"),
        ui.input_text("well_text_width", "50% text (ok)", "Some text", width="50%"),
        ui.input_select("well_select_default", "Default select (100%)", ["a","b"]),

        ui.input_slider("well_slider_width", "50% Slider (not ok, 100%)", 0, 100, 20, width="50%"),

    ui.output_text_verbatim("txt"),

def server(input, output, session):

title: Feature request: enable custom selection of ppi for plots
description:
As it stands now, the `ppi` parameter used to render all kinds of plots is globally defined here:
https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/59bbe557dc10cdacca43be2895b5e8c627572b75/shiny/render/_render.py#L191-L194

This is later on passed to all subsequent calls until either matplotlib's `savefig()` or plotnine/PIL's `save()` methods. 

Passing kwargs that end up being passed to those methods with the `@render.plot` decorator is allowed, but since the previously defined `self._ppi` is passed as an arg, adding the dpi kwarg with the decorator leads to a multiple values for argument error. 

Could it be made so that the `self._ppi` attribute is updated at instantiation time in cased it is passed as a kwarg and thus allowing more control on figure resolution?

title: Date type `ui.input_slider` breaks in double navset
description:
I've found that the `ui.input_slider` reverts to a text input field when in a double navset situation.

Working example
```
from shiny import *
from datetime import timedelta
import dateparser

min_date=dateparser.parse('12pm 3 days ago')
yesterday=dateparser.parse('12pm yesterday')
max_date=dateparser.parse('12pm today')

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.navset_pill_list(
        ui.nav("a",
            ui.input_slider(
                "date_slider",
                "Date slider",
                drag_range=True,
                min=min_date,
                max=max_date,
                value=yesterday,
                step=timedelta(hours=1)
            ),
        )
    ),
)

def server(input, output, session):
    @output(id="date_slider")
    @render.text
    def date_slider():
        input.date_slider()
        return date

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

Non-working example

title: Are there plans to support outputs displayed with IPython.display?
description:
Thanks for porting Shiny to Python - Years ago I was a user of Shiny for R and it was a really great package!

I happen to maintain a port of another great R package to Python (DT, my port is the [itables](https://github.com/mwouts/itables) project) and I was asked if that port could work under `py-shiny` (https://github.com/mwouts/itables/issues/86).

I think I could be able to implement some decorator like `render.itables`, but before undertaking that I'd like to ask if you plan to support outputs displayed with the `IPython.display` module.

It is standard practice in (Python) Jupyter notebooks to display Markdown/HTML and also Javascript components by just calling `display`. Of course if you display a single output in a cell you don't need to explicitly call `display`, but if you want to display both a Markdown header and a a dataframe you can use e.g.
```
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

display(Markdown("# Title"))
display(pd.DataFrame({'a':[5,6]}))
```
which shows the H1 title followed by the HTML table.

I think it would be a competitive advantage for Shiny for Python if these Jupyter outputs were directly supported in Shiny, because then Jupyter users would not have much to learn before they can use Shiny. AFAIK the IPython outputs are not supported in Dash by Plotly (another great package by the way), and the only dashboard system for Python that does support IPython outputs is Voila.

title: Use PyShiny, not py-shiny or for installation packages.  Hyphens in object names is not Pythonic
description: Please use the name PyShiny, not py-shiny or anything else for the names of installation packages.  This is a bad naming practice for Python packages.  Putting hyphens in the middle of a string or object name is not Pythonic, because "-" can be interpreted as a "minus sign".  Please use good Python engineering practices.  See PEP8 for more details:  https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/

title: USER REQUIREMENT: conda installation packages
description:
PyShiny is for end users doing analytics.  conda is the primary environment manager and package manager for data analytics and data science, because we need mixed language support (Python, R, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SQL, and other languages).  It is the preferred format for building robust, reproducible, and portable data science environments.  Pip is a problematic package manager because it does not do environment integrity checking. 

Please provide conda-format packages for all PyShiny tools.  This is an essential requirement.  Take the extra step to facilitate more robust application engineering.

title: UI inputs: Use a more unique name for the label's auto-generated ID
description:
When an input is created, a label tag is created along it, with an ID of `{input_ID}-label`. I've noticed this in R-Shiny but never mentioned it because it seemed too late, but since py-shiny is starting from 0 it would be nice to avoid this altogether.

I have personally seen several clients have code where they have an input with an id `test` and nearby an explanation of that input with an id of `test-label`. And I don't blame them - it can be very tempting to do so, and there's no documented reason not to.

I propose instead of using `{input_ID}-label` using something that's much less likely to be used, even if it's just adding appending a couple of underscores.

title: Incorrect `@Calc` type when function's return type is `Any`
description:
Using pyright, `Calc` works fine in cases like this:

```py
@reactive.Calc
def f():
    return 1

f  # Inferred type is (function) f: Calc_[int]
```

However, if the function returns `Any`, then it thinks that the object is a `CalcAsync_`:

```py
@reactive.Calc
def g() -> Any: ...

g  # Inferred type is (function) g: CalcAsync_[Any]
```

title: `SelectChoicesArg` shouldn't be `Optional`
description:
Commit ad9ca1b0c6b729ac925ed26fa8aee424a066b942 added the ability for `SelectChoicesArg` to be `None`, as in:

```py
input_select("x", "X", None)
```

And then when it's processed, the `None` gets transformed to `{}`.

I don't think it's particularly useful to allow a `None` here (since there's almost no reason to have a select input with no choices), and it also will cause it to behave differently from `update_select()`. With the current code, `input_select(choices=None)` means "have zero choices", but `update_select(choices=None)` means "don't change the current set of choices".

I think it's best to do what was suggested in #237, which is throw an error if `choices=None`.
