title: update_input example broken due to new choices being a tuple
description:
The update_input is erroring on `update_select`.

It looks like `_normalize_choices` [only handles lists](https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/812cec725736cebf37f1101f76c1fa32360050bd/shiny/ui/_input_select.py#L190), and returns everything else unchanged. However, the example uses `ui.input_checkbox_group()`, which seems to be returning a tuple. It seems like a tuple is the right choice for the input to return, since it is immutable.

There might be a few options for addressing.

### Option 1: Handle tuples and lists in `_normalize_choices`

pretty straightforward!

### Option 2: Convert any collections.abc.Sequence to a tuple

Alternatively you could convert any [abc.Sequence](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html) to a tuple:

```python
from collections import abc
import pandas as pd

def _normalize_choices(x):
    if isinstance(x, abc.Mapping):
        # or could check specifically for a dict
        return x
    elif isinstance(x, str):
        return {x: x}
    elif isinstance(x, abc.Sequence):
        return dict(zip(x, x))
    else:
        raise TypeError(f"Unsupported type: {type(x)}")

# okay ----
_normalize_choices("ab")
_normalize_choices(["a", "b"])
_normalize_choices(("a", "b"))
_normalize_choices({"a": 1, "b": 2})

# type error ----
_normalize_choices({"a", "b"})     # set

# pandas and numpy not handled, since they are not technically sequences
_normalize_choices(pd.Series({"x": "a", "y": "b"}))
_normalize_choices(pd.Series({"x": "a", "y": "b"}.values()))
```

### Option 3: Try to convert whatever to a tuple

```python
def _normalize_choices(x):
    # special cases ----
    if isinstance(x, dict):
        return x
    if isinstance(x, str):
        return {x: x}
    
    # general handling ----
    # will raise TypeError if can't convert to tuple
    seq = tuple(x)
    return dict(zip(seq, seq))

# all okay
_normalize_choices("ab")
_normalize_choices(["a", "b"])
_normalize_choices(("a", "b"))
_normalize_choices({"a": 1, "b": 2})
_normalize_choices({"a", "b"})

# okay. ignores index, and produces {"a": "a", "b": "b"}
# index values do not have to be unique, so they can't be converted
# to a dictionary
_normalize_choices(pd.Series({"x": "a", "y": "b"}))
_normalize_choices(pd.Series({"x": "a", "y": "b"}.values()))
```

title: Should check that generated stubs have type annotations
description:
When creating type stubs with `stubgen` and `pyright`, members which aren't explicitly annotated generally don't get a type annontation.

For example, when generating stubs with `stubgen -p shiny`, the resulting `_shinyenv.pyi` file had the following:

```py
from _typeshed import Incomplete

is_pyodide: Incomplete
```

With `pyright --create-stubs shiny`, the result is similar:

```py
is_pyodide = ...
```


The same thing happens when class instance members are defined within the init method. For example, suppose a class has something like this:

```py
class Test:
    def __init__(x: int):
        self.x = x
``

When `stubgen` generates the stub, it loses the type for `x`:

```py
from _typeshed import Incomplete

class Test:
    x: Incomplete
    def __init__(x: int) -> None: ...
```

When pyright generates the stub, it loses information about `x` completely. The result is:

```py
class Test:
    def __init__() -> None:
        ...
```

This was partially addressed in 57c39b771b32322c8c833a47339bb644f67a2261.

I think the best way to go about checking for this is to use `stubgen` in CI and search for any instances of `Incomplete`.

title: `generate_imports.py` should automate `__init.py__` generation
description:
Currently, `scripts/generate_imports.py` helps to create explicit import lists to go in the various `__init.py__` files, but they still need some manual adjustment after being generated. This process should be more automated. The same should also be used for htmltools.

Some examples of the challenges:

In `shiny/reactives/_reactives.py`, it has the following:

```
__all__ = ("Value", "Calc", "Calc_", "CalcAsync_", "Effect", "Effect_")
```

In `shiny/reactives/__init__.py`, it imports all of these, but only some of them, `("Value", "Calc", "Effect")`, are listed in the `__all__` in that file. We should add a way in `_reactives.py` to indicate which of them should be re-exported in `shiny.reactives`, and which are simply imported there.

Similarly, at the top level `shiny/__init__.py`, it imports many objects, but not all of them are explicitly re-exported.

*****

When items are not re-exported, we need to tell flake8 and pyright that it's OK. For example, in `shiny/reactive/__init__.py`:

```py
from ._reactives import (  # noqa: F401
    Value,
    Calc,
    Calc_,  # pyright: ignore[reportUnusedImport]
    CalcAsync_,  # pyright: ignore[reportUnusedImport]
    Effect,
    Effect_,  # pyright: ignore[reportUnusedImport]
)
```

description:
In R, `renderPlot()` allows you to pass whatever arugments you want to the graphics device, which is useful for things like setting a transparent bg color. 

In Python, we can't rely on passing arguments to the same function, but maybe it makes sense to pass `kwargs` along to the method that saves the file (e.g., `.savefig()` in matplotlib). At the very least, this could be useful if folks need to opt-out of the `bbox_inches="tight"` default that we'll likely set as a part of #211

title: Consider renaming/relocating `@event`
description:
The naming of the `@event` decorator feels a bit off; I think mostly because it's a reactivity concept, but it's not accessible from the `reactive` sub-package. Also, in the spirit of https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/pull/188 (where we moved all render decorators to their own sub-package), it's more convenient to just do `from shiny import reactive` instead of `from shiny import reactive, event`

Also, maybe instead of `@reactive.event()`, something like `@reactive.restrict()` would be better since it more closely ties to the underlying concept?

title: Is there an equivalent to the simplified form of R shiny's rendering without {}
description:
Looking at this example in mastering shiny:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2574498/173095732-159e4346-4e24-4b0c-9cea-de5c56521a18.png)

Do we have an analogue in py-shiny? It seems like maybe something like might be the python version (using the changes from #189):

```python
def my_cool_func(*):
    ...

def server(input, output, session):
    # approach 1
    output(lambda: my_cool_func(input$n()), name="some_output)

    # approach 2
    output(partial(my_cool_func2, input), name="some_output")
```

Now that I've written I think maybe the decorator makes sense even for wiring up simple things! (Feel free to close 😅)

title: Recalculating outputs don't fade

After the initial load of the output, move the slider.

```python
from shiny import *
import asyncio

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_slider("n", "N", 0, 100, 40),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("txt"),
)

def server(input, output, session):

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

This line

https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/3ac6afe0991a977796f8b3e37e5f6937d3d196fe/docs/sphinxext/pyshinyapp.py#L34

should probably be

That way, as long as py-shinylive is a sibling of py-shiny, building just works without setting environment variables. If we make this change though, pyshiny-site will need to set this environment variable before building

title: Build API reference fails due to recursive type definition
description:
[The 1.16.0 release of `sphinx-autodoc-typehints` broke recursive types](https://github.com/tox-dev/sphinx-autodoc-typehints/issues/223), so if you have this more recent version, you'll see:

```shell
cd docs
make clean && make html
```

```shell
Extension error (sphinx_autodoc_typehints):
Handler <function process_docstring at 0x7f9951eb01f0> for event 'autodoc-process-docstring' threw an exception (exception: maximum recursion depth exceeded)
make: *** [html] Error 2

title: reactive.Value should ignore spurious sets
description:
In R, setting a reactive value that is `identical()` to the existing value, results in the set being ignored. In Python, the same logic is implemented using `is` (object identity equality). This is different than value equality in the case of even some base types (strings, floats) and certainly any composite types.

However, using `==` is problematic also; for numpy and pandas, it means elementwise comparison and returns an iterable of bools. One approach would be to iterate over those bools, but that wouldn't detect differences in some types of metadata (e.g. pandas indices, maybe?).

Currently, the only place where we absolutely need equality comparison (that I know of) is the forthcoming `reactive.poll`. We could change `reactive.value` to never dedupe (or to dedupe only if opted in by providing a comparison function) and demand that `reactive.poll` user-provided check functions return simple data types.

title: `update_select(selected=...)` only works when choices are also provided
Should add `*` for parameters of UI elements
description:
Some UI components, like `input_select()`, have a `*` in the parameter list, before the less-commonly used parameters:

```py
def input_select(
    id: str,
    label: TagChildArg,
    choices: SelectChoicesArg,
    *,
    selected: Optional[str] = None,
    multiple: bool = False,
    selectize: bool = False,
    width: Optional[str] = None,
    size: Optional[str] = None,
) -> Tag:
```

Many other UI components do not have a `*`, but they should have one, so that we are not locked into a particular order for less-commonly used parameters. Forcing users use the names will also help with code readability.

title: debug print() calls do not flush
description:
Debug print statements, such as this one:
https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/9ee3fa9d7a0f9f7a58add1858759bca7a6b03d8a/shiny/session/_session.py#L215-L216

call `print()` without indicating that the line should be flushed.

```python
print("RECV: " + message, flush = True)
```
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#print

This means that output may be delayed in appearing downstream. We have seen some debug output delayed until process death (when any buffered pipes are fully flushed through).

title: Private random stream generates same sequence as regular random stream
description:
I took a look at the new `private_random_int()` function and I think there's a problem with the private random stream -- it simply "forks" off from the regular random stream. The result is that they return the same values. For example:

```py
import shiny
import random

str(random.randint(1, 1000))
#> '722'

shiny._utils.private_random_int(1, 1000)
#> '538'
str(random.randint(1, 1000))
#> '538'

shiny._utils.private_random_int(1, 1000)
#> '789'
str(random.randint(1, 1000))
#> '789'
```

To avoid this, I think we can use a `randint()` to seed the private random stream.

title: recommend updating pip?
description:
macOS Big Sur (11.6.5) has Python 3.8.9.

```bash
python3 --version
# => Python 3.8.9
```

Attempting to install ends up with numpy compilation errors when following the straightforward:

```bash
python3 -m venv venv
. ./venv/bin/activate
pip install shiny==0.0.0.9001 --extra-index-url=https://rstudio.github.io/pyshiny-site/pypi
```

A sampling of the errors in case it is helpful to others searching:

The root cause appears to be:

```
      numpy/core/src/multiarray/dragon4.c:3141:1: error: implicit declaration of function 'Dragon4_PrintFloat_Intel_extended128' is invalid in C99 [-Werror,-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
```

which then causes:

```
      clang: error: no such file or directory: 'build/temp.macosx-10.14-x86_64-3.8/numpy/core/src/multiarray/dragon4.o'
```

The subsequent output (and there's quite a lot) is not so helpful.

These errors can be avoided by first updating pip; after the update, the install obtains package binaries and does not appear to need compilation.

```bash
python3 -m venv venv
. ./venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install shiny==0.0.0.9001 --extra-index-url=https://rstudio.github.io/pyshiny-site/pypi
```

To be clear: This isn't a problem with this package, but encouraging a pip update will avoid what might be a common install error.

title: insert_ui() et al can't handle large messages
description:
Session dependent UI functions that utilize `session._send_message()` currently use `run_coro_sync()` to send their message in a synchronous fashion, but this problematic when the message is large...you'll get an error like (presumably, this happens because the websocket sends large messages asynchronously)

```
RuntimeError: async function yielded control; it did not finish in one iteration.
```

Here's a reprex:

```py
from shiny import *
from bokeh.resources import Resources

bokeh_js = ui.HTML(Resources(mode="inline").render())

app_ui = ui.page_fluid()

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    ui.insert_ui(ui=bokeh_js, selector="head")

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

@jcheng5 mentioned to me that it might make sense to fix this problem via `threading`

title: Proposal: `input_*` functions take a handle as a parameter, or return a handle
description:
Currently, we match up input UI components with the actual input value by using the same strings. For example, these go together:

```py
# UI component
input_text("txt", "Text input:")

# Value in server function
input.txt()
```

However, the Python type checker has no idea that these two things are related. In order to specify types for `input.txt()`, we need to do this in addition to the code above:

```py
class MyInputs(Inputs):
     txt: reactive.Value[Union[str, None]]

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    input = cast(MyInputs, input)
```

As the user modifies code, it's possible that these type definitions will get out of sync, or that there will be unused definitions (like if `txt` is removed from the app).

Here are some possible ways to make the type checker help out with checking input values.

### Option 1: modify `input_*` functions to take an `InputHandle` parameter

In the example below, the `input_num()` function takes an `InputHandle()` object as a parameter.

```py
from typing import Generic
from htmltools import *
from shiny import *

# ==========================================
# Stuff that goes in Shiny
# ==========================================
class InputHandle(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, id: str):
        self._id = id

    def __call__(self) -> T:
        s = session.get_current_session()
        if s is None:
            raise RuntimeError("No session is active.")
        x = s.input[self._id]()
        return x

# Define inputs like this
def input_num(input: InputHandle[float], label: str, value: float) -> Tag:
    return ui.input_numeric(input._id, label, value)


# ==========================================
# Usage in an app
# ==========================================
# The input ID will be "n"
input_n = InputHandle[float]("n")

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    input_num(input_n, "Enter N:", 123),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("txt")
)

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    @output()
    @render_text()
    def txt():
        return f"n*2 is {input_n() * 2}"

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

This will allow the type checker to make sure that the value of `input_n()` is the same type that an `input_num()` would provide.

One drawback here is that `input_n` still needs to be explicitly defined.


### Option 2: modify `input_*` functions to **return** an `InputHandle`

The walrus operator (`:=`) makes it possible to do assignment while passing a value to a function. For example, if our `input_num` returned an `InputHandle` object (defined slightly differently from the previous example), that `InputHandle` could be `Tagifiable`, so it could be inserted directly into the UI, **and** we could use that `InputHandle` in the server code to get the values.

```py
from typing import Generic
import htmltools
from shiny import *

# ==========================================
# Stuff that goes in Shiny
# ==========================================
class InputHandle(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, id: str, ui: htmltools.core.Tagifiable):
        self._id = id
        self._ui = ui

    def __call__(self) -> T:
        s = session.get_current_session()
        if s is None:
            raise RuntimeError("No session is active.")
        x = s.input[self._id]()
        return x

    def tagify(self) -> TagChildArg:
        return self._ui.tagify()

def input_num(id: str, label: TagChildArg, value: float) -> InputHandle[float]:
    ui_ = ui.input_numeric(id, label, value)
    return InputHandle[float](id, ui_)

# ==========================================
# Usage in an app
# ==========================================
app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    input_n := input_num("n", "N", 20),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("txt")
)

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    @output()
    @render_text()
    def txt():
        return f"n*2 is {input_n() * 2}"

app = App(app_ui, server)
```

It may even be possible to modify `input_num()` so that we don't even need to pass an ID like `"n"` -- maybe it could be autogenerated?

This method is very concise and also makes it possible to use the type checker. The one drawback I can see is that the inline definition with `:=` somewhat obscures the fact that a variable is being defined. Also, `:=` may be unfamiliar to many users, although that will likely change over time.

A similar method that doesn't make use of `:=` is maybe something like the code below. However, I'm not yet certain we can make the type checker correctly infer types from this:

```py
input = MyInputs()

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    input.n(input_num("n", "N", 20)),
)
```

*****

Open questions:

* Can we make outputs be automatically typed in a similar way?

title: Proposal: `input.x()` raise `SilentException` instead of `None` when value is not yet populated
description:
tl;dr: `req()` is supposed to be for validation and `@event()` is supposed to be for controlling reactivity, but it turns out that in some use cases `@event()` actually does a better job of validation than `req()`, which would drive users (like me) to use `@event()` when it's not quite appropriate. I propose we make `input.x()` throw a `SilentException` when the value hasn't been populated yet.

I've found myself using the following two constructs in my apps, and I think it will be a bit confusing for users to understand which one is appropriate for which uses cases:

A. `@event(input.x)`
B. `req(input.x())`

These have two different purposes:

* `@event()`: Control the triggering of reactivity
* `req()`: Validate input values.

However, it's easy to mix up the use of `@event()` and `req()`, because they overlap quite a bit in their behavior.

Here are some use cases. The first two involve controlling reactivity; the remaining three involve validation.

1. Run the code when the user clicks on a button. This works with `@event()` and `req()`.
    * Note: it works with `@event(input.x)` because we have special-cased the handling of the action button value 0. If we didn't do that, users would have to write `@event(input.x, ignore_init=True)`
2. Run the code when an input changes. This can be handled by `@event()`. `req()` does not work well because falsiness in Python is too broad, encompassing `[]`, `""`, `0`, and so on.
3. Is `input.x()` a value which will not cause an error? Usually, this means that the value is not `None`. `@event()` works here; `req()` is too broad.
4. Is `input.x()` a useful (non-falsy) value? `req()` usually works here, but not always.

In case 3 above, `@event()` is actually more useful for validating inputs than `req()`, but that's not exactly the purpose of `@event()`; using it that way would cause an Effect or output to _not_ depend on other reactive inputs.

Generally speaking, there's three kinds of validation that we're interested in:

* Is the value populated at all?
* Is the value truthy?
* Does the value satisfy some custom condition, like `input.x() > 10`?

Currently, we're expecting `req()` to do the lifting for all of these. It only does the second one natively; the first and third require extra logic, like `if input.x() is None: req(False)`.

******

Proposal:

* If `input.x()` is called before it has been populated, it throws a `SilentException`.
    * Could add an option like `input.x(throw=False)`, which causes it to return `None` instead of raising an exception.
* Add a method `input.x.ready()`, which returns `False` until the value has been populated from the client; after that it returns `True`.


Then we could simplify code like this:


```py
@output()
@render_text()
def txt():
    if input.n() is None:
       req(False)
    return f"n*2 is {input.n() * 2}"
```

Into this:

```py
@output()
@render_text()
def txt():
    return f"n*2 is {input.n() * 2}"
```

If users want a `None` for not-yet-populated values, then they can check `input.x.ready()`.

This doesn't remove the need for the third kind of validation, as in `if input.x() <= 10: req(False)`, but it's not possible to entirely get away from writing custom logic there.

Another advantage of having `input.n()` throw an exception if not yet ready is that the type can be specified more precisely. Presently, you can specify types like this:

```py
class MyInputs(Inputs):
    n: reactive.Value[Union[int, None]]

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    input = cast(MyInputs, input)
```

The `None` is necessary because it is a possible value returned by `input.n()`. But if it were to throw an exception when not ready, then we can be sure that it's always an int, which allows us to simplify it to:

```py
class MyInputs(Inputs):
    n: reactive.Value[int]
```

title: When `@event(ignore_none=True, ignore_init=True)` is used, should the initial `None` count as an initial value?
Should have simple way to declare types of input vars
description:
Currently it's possible to declare the types of input values like this:

```py
class MyInputs(Inputs):
    txt: reactive.Value[str]
    go: reactive.Value[int]

def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session):
    input = cast(MyInputs, input)
    ...
```

But it would be nice to be able to do something like this:

```py
class MyInputs(Inputs):
    txt: str
    go: int
```

Notes:
* Some inputs (like those from dynamic UI) will have a possible value of `None`
* This should inform Python that both `input.txt` and `input["txt"]` are of type `reactive.Value[str]`.

I think it should be possible to do these things. `TypedDict`, for example, does some complex stuff with types:
https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/bd8b05395ad8877f4a065562444e117b1650c022/Lib/typing.py#L2381-L2438

title: Values in `Inputs` should be read-only
Need to define `__all__` for each .py file
description:
We have files that import objects from other modules/packages but do **not** have an `__all__` specified. In those cases, the imported objects automatically get re-exported, so you can do things like this:

```py
import shiny
shiny.warn
#> <built-in function warn>
shiny.Any
#> typing.Dict
```

I believe the solution is to define `__all__` for all .py files that we have.

title: Errors when cancelling callbacks
description:
I thought of this because it's similar to #26. If a callback is cancelled during the invocation of callbacks, an error can occur.

```py
from shiny.utils import Callbacks
cb = Callbacks()

cb.register(lambda: cancel())

cancel = cb.register(lambda: print("this is a callback"))
cb.invoke()
#> KeyError: '2'
```

A different (and simpler) case: if a callback's cancel function is called after the callback has been invoked, it throws an error:

```py
from shiny.utils import Callbacks
cb = Callbacks()
cancel = cb.register(lambda: print("callback 1"), once=True)
cb.invoke()

cancel()
#> KeyError: '1'
```

import asyncio

def _():
    raise Exception("Error here!")

asyncio.run(shiny.reactcore.flush())
```

If an observer error occurs in a the server function of Shiny app, then the app crashes, which is good. However, if the observer error occurs in a Shiny app _outside_ of the server function, then nothing happens.

title: Setting `ReactiveVal` leads to `Unhandled error` in some cases
description:
The following app has a single button, which, when clicked, results in an `Unhandled error`.

```py
from shiny import *


ui = page_fluid(
    input_action_button("go", "Go"),
)

def server(session: ShinySession):
    v = ReactiveVal(0)

    @reactive()
    def r():
        print("in reactive")
        return v()

    @observe()
    def _():
        session.input["go"]   # Take a dependency on the go button

        with isolate():
            print("in observer 1-1")
            r()
            print("in observer 1-2")
            val = v()
            print("v() is " + str(val))
            print("in observer 1-3")
            v(val + 1)
            print("in observer 1-4")


    @observe()
    def _():
        print("in observer 2-1")
        r()
        print("in observer 2-2")

app = ShinyApp(ui, server)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
```

Before clicking the button, it prints this output:

```
in observer 1-1
in reactive
in observer 1-2
v() is 0
in observer 1-3
in observer 1-4
in observer 2-1
in reactive
in observer 2-2
```

When the button is clicked, this output shows up:

```
in observer 1-1
in observer 1-2
v() is 1
in observer 1-3
Unhandled error: 2763
```

So the error is happening when `v(val + 1)` is called.

Almost any change to the structure seems to make the error stop happening. For example, removing the first call to `r()` makes the error go away.

title: Methods which call `session.send_message()` crash app on pyodide
description:
On pyodide, some functions which call `session.send_message()` (like `ui_insert())` cause the app to crash with this message:

```
Unhandled error: async function yielded control; it did not finish in one iteration.
```

The problem seems to be that `session.send_message()` is wrapped in `run_coro_sync()`. This can be seen by adding `utils.run_coro_sync(s.send_message(...))` directly to an app:

```py
from shiny import *

ui = page_fluid(
    input_action_button("go", "Send message to client"),
)

def server(s: ShinySession):
    @observe()
    def _():
        if not s.input["go"]:
            return
        utils.run_coro_sync(s.send_message({"foo": "1"}))

app = ShinyApp(ui, server, debug=True)
```

This works fine when running the app normally (not in pyodide).

title: `input_*` functions crash when running in pyodide

title: Consider swapping order of choices and values for `input_radio_buttons`, `input_checkbox_group`, and `input_select`
description:
For `input_radio_buttons`, `input_checkbox_group`, and `input_select`, the choices are specified as `{"Label": "value"}`, like this:

```py
input_select("x", "Label", {"Choice A": "a", "Choice B": "b"})
```

This is a direct translation of how it's done in R. I think we should consider swapping the order, like this:

```py
input_select("x", "Label", {"a": "Choice A", "b": "Choice B"})
```

This will allow us to reduce remove the `choice_values` and `choice_names` parameters.

****

For `input_radio_buttons` and `input_checkbox_group`, the `choice_values` and `choice_names` parameters let you pass in the values and labels separately. 

```py
input_checkbox_group("x", "Label", choice_values=["a", "b"], choice_names=["Choice A", "Choice B"])
```

This comes directly from the R versions of these functions.

```R
checkboxGroupInput("x", "Label", choiceValues=c("a", "b"), choiceNames=c("Choice A", "Choice B"))
```

According to the R documentation, the purpose of the separate parameters is:

> **choiceNames, choiceValues**: List of names and values, respectively, that are displayed to the user in the app and correspond to the each choice (for this reason, choiceNames and choiceValues must have the same length). If either of these arguments is provided, then the other must be provided and choices must not be provided. The advantage of using both of these over a named list for choices is that choiceNames allows any type of UI object to be passed through (tag objects, icons, HTML code, ...), instead of just simple text. See Examples.

So in R, it lets you do this:

```R
checkboxGroupInput(
  "x",
  "Label",
  choiceValues=c("a", "b"), 
  choiceNames=list(tags$b("Choice A"), tags$i("Choice B"))
)
```

The reason that separate `choiceValues` and `choiceNames` params are needed is because you can't do `list(tags$b("Choice A")="a")`, where a complex object is the name of an element in the list:

```R
checkboxGroupInput(
  "x",
  "Label",
  choices=list(tags$b("Choice A")="a", tags$i("Choice B")="b")
)
```

IIRC, the reason for those extra parameters is because we had already established the order as `list("Choice A"="a")`, and then only later on did we consider the need for passing in complex objects as labels: https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/pull/1521

*****

For prism, we have the opportunity to swap the label and value, so users could just do this. This order also makes a bit more sense to me anyway:

```py
input_checkbox_group("x", "Label", choices={"a": tags.b("Choice A"), "b": tags.i("Choice B")})
```

The other order (the order we currently use) doesn't work, because complex objects can't be used as keys:

```py
input_checkbox_group("x", "Label", choices={tags.b("Choice A"): "a", tags.i("Choice B"): "b"})
#> TypeError: unhashable type: 'Tag'
```

This change would eliminate two parameters (`choice_names` and `choice_values`), make usage more consistent, and the `value: label` ordering just makes more sense. The only drawback that I can see is that the order is different from what we use in R.

title: docs: `ui.Theme` Shinylive examples fail — need `requirements.txt` with `shiny[theme]`
description:
## Problem

The `ui.Theme` / `express.ui.Theme` API-reference examples are broken in Shinylive on the docs site:

- https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/core/ui.Theme.html#examples
- https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/express/express.ui.Theme.html#examples

(Also reproducible on the v1.7.0 preview build: https://pr-406--pyshiny.netlify.app/api/core/ui.Theme.html)

`shared.py` builds a customized theme:

```python
my_theme = (
    ui.Theme("shiny", include_paths=Path(__file__).parent)
    .add_defaults(bslib_dashboard_design=True)
    .add_mixins(...)
    .add_rules(...)
)
```

Rendering that theme calls `Theme.to_css()`, which hits `check_theme_pkg_installed("libsass", "sass")` and raises `ImportError`, so the app never starts.

## Root cause

`sass` is imported lazily *inside* `Theme.to_css()` (`shiny/ui/_theme.py:517-518`), not at module top level. Shinylive picks packages to load by scanning the app's top-level imports, so it never sees `sass` and never loads `libsass` — even though libsass **is** bundled in Shinylive's prebuilt pyodide packages (`libsass 0.23.0` is in `pyodide-lock.json`; added in posit-dev/shinylive#160, Nov 2024, precisely to enable `ui.Theme()` in Shinylive).

The only way to get it loaded is to list it in the app's `requirements.txt`.

## Proposed fix

Add `shiny/api-examples/Theme/requirements.txt` containing:

```
shiny[theme]
```

Why this works:

- `@add_example()` already collects every non-`app-*.py`, non-`__*` file in the example dir as a support file (`shiny/_docstring.py:188-204`), so a `requirements.txt` is bundled into the Shinylive payload automatically. Precedent: `shiny/api-examples/todo_list/requirements.txt` (contains `shinyswatch`).
- Shinylive's `_install_requirements_from_dir()` reads `requirements.txt` and micropip-installs each entry, and it explicitly understands **extras on an already-installed package** — it reads the installed dist's metadata and installs just the extra's requirements. The upstream implementation literally uses our case as its worked example (`src/hooks/usePyodide.tsx`: `# Convert requires records : 'libsass>=0.23.0; extra == "theme"'`).
- `shiny[theme]` is preferable to a bare `libsass` pin because it matches what we tell users in the `ui.Theme` docstring (`pip install "shiny[theme]"`) and it tracks the extra automatically if its contents change.

### One thing to verify

`theme = ["libsass>=0.23.0", "brand_yml>=0.2.0"]`, and while `libsass` is in Shinylive's bundled pyodide packages, **`brand_yml` is not** — micropip would resolve it from PyPI (pulling `pydantic` etc.). Worth confirming the examples still load acceptably fast and don't fail offline; if `brand_yml` turns out to be a problem in wasm, fall back to a bare `libsass` in the `requirements.txt`.

## Scope

A single `requirements.txt` covers all eight app variants in the dir (`app-core.py`, `app-express.py`, and the `-local` / `-remote` / `-shinyswatch` variants), since support files are shared. No py-shiny-site change is needed — the site consumes the example dir verbatim through `make quartodoc`.

Grepping `shiny/api-examples/` turns up no other example that compiles Sass at runtime, so `Theme/` looks like the only affected one.

## Drive-by

`shiny/ui/_theme.py:733` is a plain string, not an f-string, so the error message renders literally as:

```
Please install it with `pip install {pkg}` or `pip install "shiny[theme]"`.
```

Worth fixing in the same PR.

title: Flaky test: test_input_action_task_button[firefox] (current_time output empty after 5s)
description:
Failed on [#2379](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/pull/2379) CI — a diff that touches only a release-skill reference script, so unrelated to the change. **Passed on rerun.** **Job (attempt 1):** https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/30420506896/job/90476133525 — `playwright-shiny (3.10, firefox, 1)` ## Error ``` FAILED tests/playwright/shiny/inputs/input_task_button/test_input_task_button.py::test_input_action_task_button[firefox] AssertionError: Locator expected not to be empty Actual value: empty Call log: - Expect "to_be_empty" with timeout 5000ms - waiting for locator("pre#current_time.shiny-text-output") 6 × locator resolved to 

        - unexpected value "empty"

tests/playwright/shiny/inputs/input_task_button/test_input_task_button.py:31: AssertionError
```

The failing line is the early sanity check, before any task-button interaction:

```python
y.set("4")
result = controller.OutputCode(page, "show_result")
current_time = controller.OutputCode(page, "current_time")
# Make sure the time has content
current_time.expect.not_to_be_empty()   # line 31
```

## Observation

The output stayed `recalculating` **and** empty across all 6 locator resolutions spanning the full 5000 ms default timeout. So this is not a value-mismatch race — `current_time` simply never delivered its first value inside the window.

One thing that may be relevant: `app.py` blocks the session during startup. Both event effects are declared `ignore_none=False`, so they fire on the initial flush, and `handle_click2` awaits a 1.5 s `slow_input_compute()` which (by the app's own design and comments) blocks the session:

```python
@reactive.effect
@reactive.event(input.btn_block, ignore_none=False)
async def handle_click2():
    ...
    await slow_input_compute(input.x(), input.y())   # asyncio.sleep(1.5)
```

Meanwhile `current_time` re-invalidates every 0.1 s via `reactive.invalidate_later(0.1)`. So the assertion's 5 s budget already has a ~1.5 s startup blocking window subtracted from it, and `y.set("4")` immediately beforehand adds another flush into that same window. Under Firefox + CI load that margin may simply not be enough for the first `current_time` render to arrive.

I have **not** confirmed this mechanism — the test passed on rerun and I did not reproduce it locally. Offering it only as the most plausible starting point.

## Possible directions

- Give the line-31 assertion an explicit timeout generous enough to cover the startup blocking window, rather than relying on the 5 s default.
- Or wait for the startup blocking window to clear (e.g. assert on `show_result` first, which the test already does immediately afterwards on line 34) before asserting that `current_time` is non-empty.

## Notes

- Not a v1.7.0 regression; unrelated to the release diff.
- No pre-existing issue found for this test.
- Second distinct Firefox playwright flake observed during the v1.7.0 release train; the other is #2378 (`test_auto_scroll_pinning[firefox]`). No evidence yet that they share a cause.

title: MarkdownStream auto-scroll can stall on Firefox: pinned state is derived only from async scroll events
description:
## Summary

`test_auto_scroll_pinning[firefox]` failed again on the v1.7.0 release PR CI ([#2377](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/pull/2377), a docs-only diff), and passed on rerun.

Filing this as a **new** issue rather than reopening #2351, because the interesting part is not the test — it's that the failure signature is *byte-identical* to the pre-fix occurrence, which suggests the underlying product behavior, not test timing, is the thing left unaddressed.

**Job (attempt 1):** https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/30419592356/job/90473449678 — `playwright-shiny (3.12, firefox, 2)`

```
FAILED tests/playwright/shiny/components/MarkdownStream/auto_scroll/test_stream_auto_scroll.py::test_auto_scroll_pinning[firefox]
  RuntimeError: .card-body:has(#auto_scroll_stream) never settled at bottom:
  {'scrollTop': 1998, 'scrollHeight': 2816, 'clientHeight': 258}
```

## Why this looks like more than a flake

| Occurrence | scrollTop | scrollHeight | clientHeight |
|---|---|---|---|
| #2351 (2026-07-09, **before** the #2355 fix) | 1998 | 2816 | 258 |
| This run (2026-07-29, **after** the #2355 fix) | **1998** | **2816** | **258** |

Identical geometry across three weeks and a landed fix. The container parks at exactly the pre-chunk-5 bottom — 560px short of the 2558px maximum (`scrollHeight - clientHeight`) — rather than at some arbitrary intermediate offset. A purely random timing wobble would be expected to produce varying values.

## Suspected root cause (from #2355's own analysis)

[#2355](https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/pull/2355) diagnosed this precisely and then fixed only the test side:

> the vendored `markdown-stream.js` updates its pinned/unpinned state only inside its `scroll` event handler, and `updated()` auto-scrolls only when that flag says pinned. Scroll events are dispatched asynchronously — on Firefox from paint ticks, which can lag under CI load while Playwright's timer-based polls keep running.

That fix made the *test* wait for scroll-event delivery before streaming. It did not change the design where pinned state is knowable only via an async `scroll` event. If a paint tick is late in a real browser under real load, the same stall should be reachable outside tests: `ui.MarkdownStream` silently stops following new content while appearing pinned.

## Suggested direction

Rather than widening test waits again, consider computing pinnedness on demand from live geometry at the moment `updated()` needs it (e.g. comparing `scrollTop + clientHeight` against `scrollHeight` within a tolerance), using the `scroll` handler only as a hint. That removes the dependency on event delivery timing entirely.

## Notes

- Not a v1.7.0 regression — pre-existing, and unrelated to the release diff, which touched only `CHANGELOG.md` and `CITATION.cff`.
- Supersedes/relates to #2351 (closed as completed by #2355).
- Labeled `flaky test` so it is picked up by the staleness sweep, though the argument above is that the product path deserves a look independent of the flake.

title: Flaky test: test_external_templates[database-explorer/app-core.py] fails on a conflicting DuckDB file lock
description:
## Summary

`test_external_templates[chromium-py-shiny-templates/database-explorer/app-core.py]` failed because the app could not open the template's DuckDB file — another Python process on the runner still held a conflicting lock, so the app exited before serving.

**Job (attempt 1):** https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/30473455629/job/90649156135 — `playwright-examples (3.13, chromium, 0)`. **Passed on rerun.**

```
FAILED tests/playwright/examples/test_external_templates.py::test_external_templates[chromium-py-shiny-templates/database-explorer/app-core.py]
  TimeoutError: Shiny app exited without ever becoming ready.
  Waiting for 'Uvicorn running on' in stderr. Last 20 lines of stderr:

  File ".../py-shiny-templates/database-explorer/app-core.py", line 27, in <module>
    con = duckdb.connect(str(db_file), read_only=True)

  _duckdb.IOException: IO Error: Could not set lock on file
    ".../py-shiny-templates/database-explorer/weather.db":
    Conflicting lock is held in /opt/hostedtoolcache/Python/3.13.14/x64/bin/python3.13 (PID 3103).
    See also https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/connect/concurrency
```

The test then burned its full 30s app-startup timeout (`30.00s call` in the durations list) before failing.

## Notes on the cause

Worth flagging that the failing connection is already `read_only=True`, and DuckDB permits multiple concurrent *read-only* readers — so the conflict implies the holder had it open in a mode that excludes another reader, or had not yet released it.

I did not establish which process PID 3103 was, so I want to avoid asserting a mechanism. Two plausible candidates, both concurrency-related:

1. **Sibling test still shutting down.** `test_external_templates` launches a Shiny app subprocess per parameter, and this template has both `app-core.py` and `app-express.py` opening the same `weather.db`. If the previously-run variant's app process had not fully exited when the next one started, its lock would still be held — a teardown/lock-release race rather than true simultaneity.
2. **Two xdist workers at once.** This shard ran with 2 workers (`gw0`/`gw1`); if the two variants of this template land on different workers concurrently they contend directly.

Either way the shared mutable resource is one `weather.db` in the cloned templates checkout, used by more than one test.

## Suggested direction

- Put both variants of a template in the same xdist group (`@pytest.mark.xdist_group`) so the core/express pair of a given template never runs concurrently — cheapest fix, and it also removes (2).
- Or give each test its own copy of the database (copy `weather.db` into a tmp dir per test and point the app at it), which removes the shared resource entirely and also covers (1).
- Independently: the 30s startup timeout means each occurrence costs half a minute of CI. Surfacing "app exited with an error" distinctly from "app is still starting" would fail fast here, since the process had already died.

<sub>AI-generated report. Failed on a PR whose diff was a `shiny/ui/_layout.py` refactor plus layout unit tests, unrelated to templates or DuckDB.</sub>

title: Flaky test: OTel span tests fail when xdist co-locates them (reproducible on main with -n 3)
description:
## Summary

Three OTel tests fail together when pytest-xdist happens to co-locate them on one worker:

```
FAILED tests/pytest/test_otel_reactive_execution.py::TestSpanHierarchy::test_calc_span_nested_under_reactive_update - assert 0 >= 2
FAILED tests/pytest/test_otel_reactive_flush.py::TestReactiveFlushInstrumentation::test_span_parent_child_relationship - assert 0 >= 2
FAILED tests/pytest/test_otel_reactive_flush.py::TestReactiveFlushInstrumentation::test_reactive_update_span_includes_session_id_from_context - AssertionError: reactive_update span should exist
```

**Job (attempt 1):** https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/30473455629/job/90649155012 — `check (3.14, ubuntu-latest)`. **Passed on rerun.**

The exported spans list is empty (`0 = len([])`), i.e. no spans were recorded at all — consistent with another test in the same worker process having already installed a global tracer provider.

## This is reproducible on `main`, without any PR changes

The valuable part: this does **not** require a specific diff. Checking out `origin/main` clean and co-locating the OTel test files reproduces it by varying only the worker count:

```
$ uv run pytest tests/pytest/test_otel_logfire.py \
                tests/pytest/test_otel_reactive_flush.py \
                tests/pytest/test_otel_reactive_execution.py -q -n 2
70 passed, 2 skipped

$ ... -n 3
69 passed, 1 failed, 2 skipped

$ ... -n 4
69 passed, 1 failed, 2 skipped
```

So the trigger is which OTel tests land in the same worker process, not timing jitter.

## Why it surfaces on unrelated PRs

`pytest.ini` sets `addopts = ... --numprocesses auto`. With `--dist load`, the partition of tests across workers depends on the total collected test count — so **any PR that adds or removes a test can flip which OTel tests share a process**, with no causal connection to what the PR changed.

Observed exactly that twice: adding 3 unrelated unit tests to a PR turned the full local suite from 4/4 green into 2/4 runs failing on these same tests. Adding 3 *no-op* tests instead did not trigger it — the deciding factor is the resulting partition, not the content.

The suite already knows about this coupling. `test_otel_logfire.py` self-documents it by skipping:

```
SKIPPED [1] tests/pytest/test_otel_logfire.py:55: OpenTelemetry providers already configured (likely by another test in parallel execution)
```

That skip appears or not depending on worker count too (1 skipped at `-n auto`, 2 skipped at `-n 2/3/5/6` on clean `main`) — the same root cause, just landing on the more graceful branch. `test_otel_value_logging.py`'s session-scoped fixture docstring also calls out that OTel uses a global singleton provider and that `set_logger_provider()` cannot be called twice.

## Suggested direction

The tests that assert on span contents depend on owning the global tracer provider, but nothing enforces that ownership. Options, roughly in increasing robustness:

1. Give the span-asserting tests the same defensive skip `test_otel_logfire.py` uses — cheap, but converts failures into silently-skipped coverage.
2. Pin all OTel test files to one xdist worker (`--dist loadfile`/`loadgroup` via `@pytest.mark.xdist_group`), so co-location becomes deterministic rather than luck.
3. Stop relying on the process-global provider in these tests — use an isolated `TracerProvider` per test and read spans from its own exporter, instead of whatever the global happens to be.

(3) removes the coupling; (2) makes it deterministic and is a much smaller change.

<sub>AI-generated report. Failed on a PR whose diff was a `shiny/ui/_layout.py` refactor plus layout unit tests, unrelated to OTel.</sub>

title: Remove Pyright: stub generation can move to `pyrefly stubgen`, but needs pyrefly >= 1.2.0
description:
## Background

Following #2368, Pyrefly is the primary type checker (`make check-types` → `check-pyrefly`) and `pyrefly-baseline.json` is down to `{"errors": []}`. Pyright, however, is still fully wired in:

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| `pyrightconfig.json` | still present, `typeCheckingMode: "strict"` |
| `pyproject.toml:144` | `pyright>=1.1.407` dev dependency |
| `Makefile:59-67` | `pyright --createstub folium/uvicorn/seaborn` |
| `Makefile:75` | `pyright-typings`, a prerequisite of **both** `check-pyright` **and** `check-pyrefly` |
| `Makefile:93-95`, `Makefile:107` | `check-pyright` / `pyright` targets |
| `.github/workflows/pytest.yaml:70-87` | dedicated `Pyright` CI job, listed as a required check at line 433 |
| `pyproject.toml:227-229` | `permissive-ignores = true`, kept solely so Pyrefly honors `# pyright: ignore` |
| source tree | **1463** `# pyright: ignore` comments (vs 127 `# pyrefly: ignore`), across 481 of 1189 `.py` files, plus ~40 file-level rule toggles and 4 `# pyright: basic` |

There are two independent blockers to removing it. This issue tracks the first, which is now understood; the second is noted at the bottom.

## Blocker 1: stub generation (investigated)

`make pyright-typings` shells out to `pyright --createstub` for folium, uvicorn, and seaborn, so Pyright can't be dropped until stub generation is replaced. (matplotlib stubs come from a `git clone` of microsoft/python-type-stubs and are unaffected.)

[`pyrefly stubgen`](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/stubgen/) is a viable replacement, but **only on an unreleased version**.

### What was verified

Generated stubs for all three packages with each tool, swapped them into `typings/`, and ran both checkers:

| `typings/` generated by | `pyrefly check` | `pyright` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pyright --createstub` (current) | 0 errors | 0 errors |
| `pyrefly 1.1.1 stubgen` | 0 errors | **10 errors** |
| `pyrefly 1.2.0.dev3 stubgen` | 0 errors | **3 errors** |
| `pyrefly 1.2.0.dev3 stubgen --include-private` | 0 errors | 0 errors |

Two distinct stubgen bugs account for the failures.

**1. `__all__` is dropped from emitted stubs** (7 of the 10 errors)

`uvicorn/supervisors/__init__.pyi` loses `__all__ = ["Multiprocess", "ChangeReload"]`. Per the typing spec, a name imported in a stub via `from X import Y` is not re-exported unless it appears in `__all__` or is written `from X import Y as Y`, so `shiny/_uvicorn.py:14` fails with `"Multiprocess" is unknown import symbol`.

This is systemic, not uvicorn-specific: **0** of the stubs generated by 1.1.1 contained `__all__`, against 17 from Pyright across the 18 source modules that define it.

Fixed upstream in facebook/pyrefly#3924, closed 2026-06-26 (commit `9752acc`). Pyrefly **1.1.1 shipped 2026-06-18**, so the fix has never appeared in a stable release — it's only in `1.2.0.dev*`. With `1.2.0.dev3`, `__all__` coverage matches or beats Pyright (seaborn: 13 in source, 12 from Pyright, 13 from stubgen).

**2. Private symbols are dropped while public aliases still reference them** (remaining 3 errors)

`uvicorn/_types.py` defines:

```python
class _WebSocketReceiveEventBytes(TypedDict): ...
class _WebSocketReceiveEventText(TypedDict): ...
WebSocketReceiveEvent = _WebSocketReceiveEventBytes | _WebSocketReceiveEventText
```

stubgen emits the public alias but omits both underscore-prefixed classes, leaving dangling references that resolve to `Unknown` and trip Pyright strict's `reportUnknownVariableType` in `shiny/_uvicorn.py` and `shiny/_main/_run.py`.

Passing `--include-private` works around this. I don't see an upstream issue for it — worth filing separately.

### Proposed change, once pyrefly 1.2.0 is stable

Bump to `pyrefly>=1.2.0` and replace the three `typings/*` recipes in `Makefile:59-67`. Resolve package paths without hardcoding a Python version (verified working):

```make
typings/folium:
	@echo "Creating folium stubs"
	pyrefly stubgen "$$(python -c "import importlib.util as u,os;print(os.path.dirname(u.find_spec('folium').origin))")" \
		-o typings/folium --include-private
```

Runtime is comparable — roughly 7-9s per package.

### Note

`pyrefly check` reported `0 errors (207 suppressed)` in *every* configuration above, including the two broken ones. Pyrefly does not enforce the stub re-export rule, so it cannot detect this class of stub degradation; Pyright was the only thing that caught either bug. That's an argument for keeping the Pyright CI job for a while even after stubgen lands, rather than removing it in the same PR.

## Blocker 2: shinylive typings (not yet investigated)

`.github/workflows/pytest.yaml:71-73` says the separate Pyright job stays *"until shinylive's typings are validated under Pyrefly."* That's independent of stub generation and is the blocker that actually gates removal today. It needs its own investigation.

## Suggested sequencing

1. File the `--include-private` bug upstream.
2. Wait for pyrefly 1.2.0 stable; migrate `pyright-typings` → `pyrefly stubgen`. Pyright is then no longer *required to run Pyrefly*, though its CI job can stay.
3. Investigate and resolve the shinylive typings question.
4. Remove the Pyright job, `pyrightconfig.json`, and the dev dependency.
5. Convert `# pyright: ignore` → `# pyrefly: ignore` (preferring specific rule codes), then flip `permissive-ignores = false` — as already noted in `pyproject.toml:228`.
6. Update the docs that still name Pyright as the type checker: `CLAUDE.md:23,100,128-129,175`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md:64,85,294,317`, `.claude/skills/port-from-bslib/SKILL.md:338`.

title: content_type="semi-markdown" exists in the client but not in StreamingContentType
description:
## Problem

The client accepts a `content_type` value that the Python API does not expose: `"semi-markdown"`.

**Client** — `shiny/www/py-shiny/markdown-stream/markdown-stream.js` handles four values, dispatching `semi-markdown` to a different `marked` renderer than `markdown`:

```js
if (e === "markdown") { ... renderer: uo ... }
else if (e === "semi-markdown") { ... renderer: po ... }   // distinct renderer
else if (e === "html") { ... }
else if (e === "text") { return t; }
else throw new Error(`Unknown content type: ${e}`);
```

**Python** — `shinychat/_markdown_stream.py` L20:

```python
StreamingContentType = Literal[
    "markdown",
    "html",
    "text",
]
```

Nothing under `shiny/ui/` mentions `semi-markdown`.

## Consequence

Passing `content_type="semi-markdown"` works at runtime (`Literal` is not enforced) but fails type checking, and is undiscoverable from the Python side. The `po` renderer appears to be the HTML-escaping variant, which is a genuinely useful mode for streaming untrusted LLM output — so this is a real capability that is currently reachable only by accident.

## Suggested resolution

Pick one:

1. **Expose it** — add `"semi-markdown"` to `StreamingContentType` and document what it does differently from `"markdown"` (escaping behavior). Preferred if the escaping mode is intentional.
2. **Remove it** — drop the branch from the JS if it is a vestigial port from R Shiny.

Either way the two sides should agree.

Context: the docs site briefly documented `"semi-markdown"` as a valid value and removed it after discovering it was absent from the Python signature (posit-dev/py-shiny-site#418). Verified against `shiny` 1.7.1.dev6.

title: render.download_button()/download_link() cannot pass icon, class_ or style
description:
## Problem

`@render.download_button()` and `@render.download_link()` auto-place their control, which is what makes the Express one-liner work. But they accept only:

```
filename, media_type, encoding, label, width
```

There is no `icon`, and no way to pass `class_` / `style` / other attributes through to the generated control — even though `ui.download_button()` / `ui.download_link()` accept all of them.

## Consequence

An Express user who wants an icon (or a `btn-success` class) has to abandon the one-liner, place the control by hand, *and* learn `ui.hold()` to suppress the duplicate that the decorator would otherwise auto-place:

```python
from shiny.express import render, ui
from shiny.ui import download_button   # NB: shiny.express.ui has no download_* at all

download_button(
    "download",
    "Download Report",
    icon=ui.tags.i(class_="fa-solid fa-file-arrow-down"),
)

with ui.hold():  # suppress the auto-placed duplicate button
    @render.download_button(filename="report.txt")
    def download():
        yield "..."
```

Two extra concepts (`ui.hold()`, and knowing the auto-placement exists at all) for one icon.

## Suggested enhancement

Forward `**kwargs` — or at minimum `icon` — from the decorator to `auto_output_ui()`, so this works:

```python
@render.download_button(filename="report.txt", icon=ui.tags.i(class_="fa-solid fa-download"))
def download():
    yield "..."
```

## Why it matters for the docs

The Shiny for Python docs site currently has to teach the `ui.hold()` pattern on both the [Download Button](https://shiny.posit.co/py/components/inputs/download-button/) and [Download Link](https://shiny.posit.co/py/components/inputs/download-link/) kitchen-sink examples purely to demonstrate `icon` and `class_`. If the decorator forwarded these, those examples would collapse back to a single decorator and the pages would not need to introduce `ui.hold()` at all.

Also worth noting: `shiny.express.ui` exports **no** download functions (`dir()` shows none), so the explicit-placement path additionally requires importing from `shiny.ui` inside an Express app — an easy thing to get wrong.

Found while documenting these components (posit-dev/py-shiny-site#385, #386). Verified against `shiny` 1.7.1.dev6.

title: docs: panel_conditional() docstring documents an id that cannot exist
description:
## Problem

The `panel_conditional()` docstring documents a workaround for an input id that cannot exist.

`shiny/ui/_bootstrap.py` L161-162:

> ... the input id's, but if you do use them anyway, for example, `id = "foo.bar"`, you will have to use `input["foo.bar"]` instead of ``input.foo.bar`` to read the input

But Shiny rejects any id outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, so `"foo.bar"` can never be created in the first place:

```python
>>> from shiny._namespaces import resolve_id
>>> resolve_id("foo.bar")
ValueError: The string 'foo.bar' is not a valid id; only letters, numbers, and underscore are permitted
```

(`shiny/_namespaces.py` — `re_valid_id = re.compile("^\\.?\\w+$")`, enforced by `validate_id()`.)

So the advice is unreachable: a reader can never be in the situation it describes.

## Additional context

The one case where bracket syntax *would* seem necessary — module namespacing, where the real DOM id is `mod-show` — is handled automatically. `panel_conditional` emits `data-ns-prefix="mod-"` and the client narrows the `input` scope, so inside a module you write the **plain** id:

```python
# Inside a module — correct:
ui.panel_conditional("input.show", ...)

# Does NOT work:
ui.panel_conditional("input['mod-show']", ...)
```

Verified both directions in a running app.

## Suggested fix

Delete that sentence. Optionally replace it with a note that module-scoped conditions use the plain (unprefixed) id, since that is the question the current text looks like it is answering.

Found while documenting `panel_conditional` on the docs site (posit-dev/py-shiny-site#414). Verified against `shiny` 1.7.1.dev6.

title: docs: navbar_options() docstring uses `class=`, which is a SyntaxError
description:
## Problem

The `navbar_options()` docstring shows `class=` as a keyword argument. `class` is a Python reserved word, so copy-pasting any of these examples raises `SyntaxError`.

`shiny/ui/_navs.py`:

- **L1122** — ``navbar_options=ui.navbar_options(class="bg-primary", theme="dark")``
- **L1126** — prose: ``This particular combination of `class="bg-primary"` and `theme="dark"` works well``
- **L1136** — ``navbar_options = ui.navbar_options(class="bg-light", theme="light")``

## Reproducer

```python
from shiny import ui

# Copy-pasted from the docstring:
ui.navbar_options(class="bg-primary", theme="dark")
#                 ^ SyntaxError: invalid syntax
```

## Expected

`class_=`, which is the htmltools convention for reserved-word attributes.

Verified that `class_=` works and lands as expected on the rendered element:

```
class="navbar navbar-expand-md bg-primary" data-bs-theme="dark"
```

## Fix

Change the two code blocks to `class_=`, and the prose mention at L1126 to match. These render into the published API reference, so the broken form is user-visible at <https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/core/ui.navbar_options.html>.

Found while documenting `navbar_options` on the docs site (posit-dev/py-shiny-site#414). Verified against `shiny` 1.7.1.dev6.

title: [Bug]: `shiny.module` re-exports are stripped from generated type stubs, so Pyright rejects them in Shinylive
description: ## Summary In the Shinylive editor, these imports are flagged as errors even though the code runs correctly: ```python from shiny.module import resolve_id # "resolve_id" is unknown import symbol from shiny.module import current_namespace # "current_namespace" is unknown import symbol from shiny.module import ResolvedId # "ResolvedId" is unknown import symbol ``` This came up while working on some doc changes in https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny-site/pull/436. For example: `shiny/module.py` re-exports these names from `shiny._namespaces` but never references them in its own body. `pyright --createstub` drops imports that aren't referenced, so the generated `shiny/module.pyi` still advertises the names in `__all__` while never importing them. Shinylive bundles those stubs for its in-browser Pyright (via `scripts/create_typeshed.py` in the shinylive repo), so the documented import surfaces a spurious error. This is editor-only. Runtime behavior is correct. ## Evidence The stub actually shipped in the shinylive 0.10.14 assets (`shinylive/pyright/typeshed.en.json` → `/src/typings/shiny/module.pyi`): ```python from typing import Callable, TYPE_CHECKING, TypeVar from ._docstring import add_example from ._namespaces import Id # ← only Id survived from ._typing_extensions import Concatenate, ParamSpec from .session import Inputs, Outputs, Session __all__ = ("current_namespace", "resolve_id", "ui", "server", "ResolvedId") ``` `shiny/_namespaces.pyi` in the same bundle defines `resolve_id`, `current_namespace`, and `ResolvedId` correctly — only the re-export hop through `shiny/module.py` is lost. Status of every name in `shiny.module.__all__`: | Name | Stub status | Why | |---|---|---| | `current_namespace` | broken | re-export only | | `resolve_id` | broken | re-export only | | `ResolvedId` | broken | re-export only | | `ui` | OK | defined in `module.py` | | `server` | OK | defined in `module.py` | `Id` survives only because of the existing workaround at `shiny/module.py:23-24`: ```python # Ensure that Id type is not stripped out from .pyi file when generating type stubs _: Id # type: ignore ``` which suggests this was hit once already and patched for a single symbol. ## Reproduction Any Shinylive example using the documented import reproduces it. Minimal standalone repro of the stub generation, with a package mirroring `module.py`'s re-export pattern: ```python # mypkg/module.py __all__ = ("current_namespace", "resolve_id", "ui", "server", "ResolvedId") from ._namespaces import Id, ResolvedId, current_namespace, namespace_context, resolve_id _: Id # type: ignore def ui(fn): ... ``` ```bash pyright --createstub mypkg && cat typings/mypkg/module.pyi ``` Output keeps only `from ._namespaces import Id`; the other three names are dropped while `__all__` still lists them. ## Options tested (pyright 1.1.411) | Approach | Result | |---|---| | Current form (plain import + `__all__`) | Reproduces the bug; only `Id` retained | | PEP 484 redundant alias — `import resolve_id as resolve_id` | **Regresses** — entire import line dropped, `Id` lost too | | Annotation probe — `_r: ResolvedId` | Retains *type* symbols | | Module-level assignment — `_keep = (resolve_id, ...)` | Does **not** retain functions (RHS elided to `...`) | | Defining thin wrappers in `module.py` | Emits real `def resolve_id(...)` / `def current_namespace(...)` | Worth calling out: the redundant-alias form is the idiomatic PEP 484 re-export fix and is the natural first thing to reach for, but it makes this *worse* under `--createstub`. ## Suggested fix Annotations retain type symbols; they can't retain functions, and assignments don't either. So the two categories need different handling in `shiny/module.py`: 1. **`ResolvedId`** — extend the existing annotation workaround: ```python _r: ResolvedId # type: ignore ``` 2. **`resolve_id` / `current_namespace`** — define thin delegating wrappers so `createstub` emits real function signatures: ```python def resolve_id(id: Id) -> ResolvedId: """Resolve an ID, possibly with a module namespace.""" return _namespaces.resolve_id(id) ``` Both were verified to produce a correct stub. A wrapper adds one call of indirection; if that's unwanted, the alternative is fixing it on the shinylive side (post-process the generated stubs, or don't use `--createstub` for `shiny`) — happy to move this issue there if that's the better venue. ## Impact `from shiny.module import resolve_id` is the documented public API for making custom components and hand-written HTML ids module-aware (see the "Custom JavaScript component" docs page and the modules article). Anyone following those docs in Shinylive gets a red squiggle on correct code. ## Environment - shiny `1.7.1.dev6` (py-shiny `f85a444`); the pattern is unchanged in current `main` - shinylive JS assets `0.10.14` (via shinylive PyPI `0.8.11`) - pyright `1.1.411` - Runtime unaffected — apps using these imports run correctly

title: Flaky CI: playwright-examples fails with TargetClosedError from remote Playwright server
description:
Every test in the `playwright-examples` shard failed at setup with `TargetClosedError: Browser.new_page: Target page, context or browser has been closed`. Re-running the same job on the same commit passed.

- Failed job: https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/31183101660/job/92880938160
- Commit: `61542d3f` (PR #2416)
- Job: `playwright-examples (3.14, chromium, 0)` (run attempt 1)
- Re-run of the same job on the same commit: passed (run attempt 2)

## Error

```
_ ERROR at setup of test_api_examples[chromium-shiny/api-examples/include_js/app-core.py] _
[gw0] linux -- Python 3.14.6 /home/runner/work/py-shiny/py-shiny/.venv/bin/python3

tests/playwright/conftest.py:141: in page
    session_page = _new_session_page(browser)
tests/playwright/conftest.py:48: in _new_session_page
    page = browser.new_page()
E   playwright._impl._errors.TargetClosedError: Browser.new_page: Target page, context or browser has been closed
.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/playwright/_impl/_connection.py:632: TargetClosedError
```

Every xdist worker (`gw0`, `gw1`, `gw2`) hit the same error on its very first test, so the whole shard cascaded into ~90 setup errors.

## Notes

This looks like an infra race in the remote Playwright server setup (`.github/py-shiny/setup-playwright-remote/action.yaml`), not a test-code bug. That action starts a `playwright run-server` container, then a "Wait for Playwright server" readiness check that connects a browser and explicitly calls `browser.close()` to confirm the server is up. If `run-server` shares/reuses a single browser instance across client connections rather than launching a fresh one per connection, that `close()` can tear down the browser that the real pytest-xdist workers then attach to, leaving them with an already-closed `Browser` object — matching the immediate, first-test failure across every worker.

The same failure signature (`TargetClosedError: Browser.new_page: ... has been closed`) also appears on `main`, e.g. run https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/30800183463/job/91642712834 (2026-08-03), so this predates PR #2416 and isn't caused by its (docs-only) changes.

title: Flaky: test_api_examples[webkit-shiny/api-examples/todo_list/app-core.py] — resource 404 in console
description:
## Occurrence

- Job: https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/31414916798/job/93541539114
- Job name: `playwright-examples (3.12, webkit, 1)`
- Test: `tests/playwright/examples/test_api_examples.py::test_api_examples[webkit-shiny/api-examples/todo_list/app-core.py]`
- Date: 2026-08-10
- Seen on: PR #2428 (a docstring-only commit)

## Error

```
E           AssertionError: In app shiny/api-examples/todo_list/app-core.py had JavaScript console errors!
E           Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)

tests/playwright/examples/example_apps.py:258: AssertionError
========= 1 failed, 96 passed, 4 skipped, 3 rerun in 110.79s (0:01:50) =========
```

The assertion is the `console_errors` check in `example_apps.py:258`. Note the `3 rerun` — the in-job `pytest-rerunfailures` retries were exhausted, so this reproduced several times within the one job before surfacing.

## Why this looks like a flake

- **Passed on restart.** `gh run rerun 31414916798 --failed` came back fully green (173 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed) with no code change in between.
- The failure is a **static resource 404 in the browser console**, not an app-level Python error, and the commit under test changed only docstrings.
- The immediately preceding head on the same branch was fully green at 173 passed.

## Notes

The console message does not identify which resource 404'd, which is the main obstacle to diagnosing this. If it recurs, capturing the failing request URL (e.g. logging `console_errors` alongside the page's failed network requests in `example_apps.py`) would make the next occurrence actionable — a webkit-only asset race on app startup is the leading guess.

title: Flaky test: test_date_range_input[app-express.py-firefox] — Page.goto(about:blank) timeout at setup
description:
`playwright-ai (3.10, firefox, 0)` failed at **setup** for a single test, timing out while navigating the fresh page to `about:blank` — before any Shiny app was loaded. Re-running the same job on the same commit passed.

- Failed job: https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/31413230496/job/93536027091 (run attempt 1)
- Re-run of the same job on the same commit: passed (run attempt 2)
- Commit: `f41c80e8` (PR #2429)
- Job: `playwright-ai (3.10, firefox, 0)`

## Error

```
ERROR tests/playwright/ai_generated_apps/bookmark/input_date_range/test_input_date_range_express_bookmarking.py::test_date_range_input[app-express.py-firefox]

tests/playwright/conftest.py:143: in page
    session_page.goto("about:blank")
tests/playwright/conftest.py:58: in goto_and_verify_commit
    response = original_goto(url, **kwargs)
...
E  playwright._impl._errors.TimeoutError: Page.goto: Timeout 30000ms exceeded.
E  Call log:
E    - navigating to "about:blank", waiting until "load"
```

Result for the shard: `40 passed, 1 error in 135.88s`.

## Notes

The navigation that timed out is to `about:blank`, so no app code is involved — this is browser/remote-server startup latency, not a problem with the app under test. (`input_date_range/app-express.py` does not use `expressify`, and the sibling Express bookmark apps that *do* — `accordion`, `navsets` — passed in the same job.)

Supporting evidence that the runner was simply very slow: the three slowest durations in the shard were all *setup*, at 83s, 73s, and 58s, against a 30s `goto` timeout. Earlier in the log there are also several `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed` / `Connection.init: Event loop is closed` tracebacks from Playwright teardown.

Possibly the same underlying infrastructure issue as #2424 (`playwright-examples` failing with `TargetClosedError` from the remote Playwright server), though the signature differs: there, `browser.new_page()` raised `TargetClosedError` and every worker in the shard cascaded; here a single test timed out inside `page.goto()`.

title: Flaky test: test_tooltip_demo[app-express.py-webkit] — tooltip body not found after update
description:
## Occurrence

- Failed job: https://github.com/posit-dev/py-shiny/actions/runs/31397735515/job/93484713496 (`playwright-ai (3.14, webkit, 1)`, on PR #2415)
- Passed on `gh run rerun --failed` of the same commit, so this is a flake rather than a regression. `main` was green at the time.
- Result in the original job: `1 failed, 43 passed in 73.94s`

## Test

`tests/playwright/ai_generated_apps/core_express/update_tooltip/test_update_tooltip_core_express.py::test_tooltip_demo[app-express.py-webkit]`

Only the `webkit` + Express parameterization failed; the other browsers and the Core app variant passed in the same run.

## Error

```
>       playwright_expect(self.get_loc_overlay_body(timeout=timeout)).to_have_text(
            value, timeout=timeout
        )
E       AssertionError: Locator expected to have text 'Tooltip updated 2 times!'
E       Actual value: None
E       Error: element(s) not found
E       Call log:
E         - Expect "to_have_text" with timeout 5000ms
E         - waiting for locator("#None.tooltip > div.tooltip-inner")

.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/shiny/playwright/controller/_overlay.py:112: AssertionError
```

Aria snapshot at failure time shows the page rendered and the trigger buttons present, but no tooltip overlay in the DOM:

```
- heading "Update Tooltip Demo" [level=2]
- text: Tooltip Demo
- button " Show tooltip"
- button " Close tooltip"
- button " Update tooltip"
- separator
- button " Hover over me!"
```

## Notes

Two things stand out in the call log and may be worth a look beyond the timing flake itself:

- The locator is `#None.tooltip > div.tooltip-inner` — the `None` suggests the overlay controller resolved a placeholder id rather than the real tooltip id, so the selector may be unable to match even when the overlay *is* present. Worth confirming whether `_overlay.py`'s `get_loc_overlay_body()` is constructing the selector correctly for this app.
- The assertion waits for the *updated* text ("Tooltip updated 2 times!") with the overlay expected to already be open; on webkit the show/update sequence may race, leaving the overlay closed at assertion time.
